**Martin Kiptolo Lel** (born 29 October 1978) is a Kenyan professional [long distance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_track_event "Long-distance track event") and [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon_race "Marathon race") runner. He won the [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Marathon "London Marathon") in 2005, 2007, and 2008, the [New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Marathon "New York City Marathon") in 2003 and 2007 and the [Great North Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_North_Run "Great North Run") in 2007 and 2009. His personal best time, as of April 2008[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Martin_Lel&action=edit), is 2:05:15, which he ran in the 2008 London Marathon setting a course record.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Lel#cite_note-1) Lel is coached by [Claudio Berardelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claudio_Berardelli?action=edit&redlink=1 "Claudio Berardelli (page does not exist)") and lives in the [Rift Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rift_Valley_Province "Rift Valley Province") region of Kenya.

Lel ran his first marathons in 2002: he failed to finish at the [Prague Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prague_Marathon "Prague Marathon"), but in his first finish he managed to claim second in the [Venice Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice_Marathon "Venice Marathon").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Lel#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Lel#cite_note-3) He won [Lisbon Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon_Half_Marathon "Lisbon Half Marathon") in 2003, 2006 and 2009,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Lel#cite_note-4) was the [gold medalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_medal "Gold medal") at the [2003 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "2003 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships"), and won the [Portugal Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portugal_Half_Marathon "Portugal Half Marathon") in 2005. He made his Olympic debut for Kenya at the [2008 Beijing Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Beijing_Olympics "2008 Beijing Olympics") and came fifth in the marathon.

He beat [Samuel Wanjiru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru "Samuel Wanjiru") to win the inaugural edition of the [Rock ‘n’ Roll Mardi Gras Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_%E2%80%98n%E2%80%99_Roll_Mardi_Gras_Marathon "Rock ‘n’ Roll Mardi Gras Marathon") in 2010.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Lel#cite_note-5) In August 2010, he ran at the [Falmouth Road Race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falmouth_Road_Race "Falmouth Road Race") and took third place.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Lel#cite_note-6) After almost 3 years without running a marathon, he participated in the [2011 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_London_Marathon "2011 London Marathon") as a replacement for Samuel Wanjiru, who was originally invited to run, but he still placed second with a time of 2:05:45, out-sprinting [Patrick Makau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Makau "Patrick Makau") at the finish line.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Lel#cite_note-7) He ran the 15K [Saint Silvester Road Race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Silvester_Road_Race "Saint Silvester Road Race") at the end of the year, but was beaten into fourth place.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Lel#cite_note-8) Lel entered two races the year after: he was runner-up again at the [2012 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_London_Marathon "2012 London Marathon") (finishing in 2:06:51) and was victorious at the [Portugal Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portugal_Half_Marathon "Portugal Half Marathon") with a time of 61:28 minutes.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Lel#cite_note-9)

In 2011, the American Charity, Shoe4Africa, funded and opened the [Shoe4Africa Martin Lel school](http://allafrica.com/stories/201412301225.html) in Lel's home village, Kimn'geru, to honor the athlete.

His brother, [Cyprian Kimurgor Kotut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyprian_Kimurgor_Kotut "Cyprian Kimurgor Kotut"), followed in his footsteps as a marathon runner and won the 2016 Paris Marathon.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Lel#cite_note-DN-10)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Kenyan long-distance runner

Martin Lel

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5d/20060423_Felix_Limo_and_Martin_Lel.jpg/250px-20060423_Felix_Limo_and_Martin_Lel.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:20060423_Felix_Limo_and_Martin_Lel.jpg)

Martin Lel (right) at the 2006 [London Marathon](link_3)
Personal information
Nationality![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/Flag_of_Kenya.svg/40px-Flag_of_Kenya.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)[Kenya](link_4)
Born(1978-10-29) 29 October 1978 (age 47)

[Kapsabet](link_5), [Kenya](link_4)
Height 5 ft 7 in (1.70 m)
Weight 54 kg (119 lb)

**Martin Kiptolo Lel** (born 29 October 1978) is a Kenyan professional [long distance](link_6) and [marathon](link_7) runner. He won the [London Marathon](link_3) in 2005, 2007, and 2008, the [New York City Marathon](link_8) in 2003 and 2007 and the [Great North Run](link_9) in 2007 and 2009. His personal best time, as of April 2008[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Martin_Lel&action=edit), is 2:05:15, which he ran in the 2008 London Marathon setting a course record.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Lel#cite_note-1) Lel is coached by [Claudio Berardelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claudio_Berardelli?action=edit&redlink=1 "Claudio Berardelli (page does not exist)") and lives in the [Rift Valley](link_10) region of Kenya.

Lel ran his first marathons in 2002: he failed to finish at the [Prague Marathon](link_11), but in his first finish he managed to claim second in the [Venice Marathon](link_12).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Lel#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Lel#cite_note-3) He won [Lisbon Half Marathon](link_14) in 2003, 2006 and 2009,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Lel#cite_note-4) was the [gold medalist](link_15) at the [2003 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships](link_16), and won the [Portugal Half Marathon](link_18) in 2005. He made his Olympic debut for Kenya at the [2008 Beijing Olympics](link_19) and came fifth in the marathon.

He beat [Samuel Wanjiru](link_20) to win the inaugural edition of the [Rock ‘n’ Roll Mardi Gras Marathon](link_22) in 2010.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Lel#cite_note-5) In August 2010, he ran at the [Falmouth Road Race](link_23) and took third place.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Lel#cite_note-6) After almost 3 years without running a marathon, he participated in the [2011 London Marathon](link_24) as a replacement for Samuel Wanjiru, who was originally invited to run, but he still placed second with a time of 2:05:45, out-sprinting [Patrick Makau](link_25) at the finish line.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Lel#cite_note-7) He ran the 15K [Saint Silvester Road Race](link_26) at the end of the year, but was beaten into fourth place.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Lel#cite_note-8) Lel entered two races the year after: he was runner-up again at the [2012 London Marathon](link_27) (finishing in 2:06:51) and was victorious at the [Portugal Half Marathon](link_18) with a time of 61:28 minutes.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Lel#cite_note-9)

In 2011, the American Charity, Shoe4Africa, funded and opened the [Shoe4Africa Martin Lel school](link_28) in Lel's home village, Kimn'geru, to honor the athlete.

His brother, [Cyprian Kimurgor Kotut](link_29), followed in his footsteps as a marathon runner and won the 2016 Paris Marathon.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Lel#cite_note-DN-10)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Tanzanian long-distance runner

**Fabiano Joseph Naasi** (born December 24, 1985, in [Babati](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babati "Babati"), [Manyara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manyara "Manyara")) is a Tanzanian long-distance runner.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Tanzanian long-distance runner

**Fabiano Joseph Naasi** (born December 24, 1985, in [Babati](link_2), [Manyara](link_3)) is a Tanzanian long-distance runner.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Wilson Kiprop

[![Image 1](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dd/Wilson_Kiprop.jpg/250px-Wilson_Kiprop.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wilson_Kiprop.jpg)
Kiprop at the 2012 Olympics
Personal information
Nationality![Image 2: Kenya](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/Flag_of_Kenya.svg/40px-Flag_of_Kenya.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)[Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya")
Born 14 April 1987 (age 39)
Sport
Sport[Long-distance running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_running "Long-distance running")
Events[10,000 m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_m "10,000 m"), [Half marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon "Half marathon"), [Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon")
Coached by[Renato Canova](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renato_Canova "Renato Canova")

**Wilson Kiprop** (born 14 April 1987 in Soi, [Uasin Gishu District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uasin_Gishu_District "Uasin Gishu District"))[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-1) is a Kenyan [long-distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_running "Long-distance running"), who specialises in the [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres "10,000 metres") and [half marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon "Half marathon"). He was the world champion at the [IAAF World Half Marathon Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics_Championships "World Athletics Championships") in 2010 and was the 10,000 m [gold medalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_medal "Gold medal") at the [2010 African Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_African_Championships_in_Athletics "2010 African Championships in Athletics").

He started competing at the top level in 2008, winning competitions in Italy ([cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-country_running "Cross-country running") and [road races](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_running "Road running")) and working under two Italian coaches, [Renato Canova](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renato_Canova "Renato Canova") and Gabriele Nicola. He was the 2008 champion at the [Cross della Vallagarina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_della_Vallagarina "Cross della Vallagarina") and the [Corrida di San Geminiano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corrida_di_San_Geminiano?action=edit&redlink=1 "Corrida di San Geminiano (page does not exist)").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-3) The following year he won the Vallagarina race for a second time running and came first at the [Eurocross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurocross "Eurocross") and [Trofeo Sant'Agata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trofeo_Sant'Agata?action=edit&redlink=1 "Trofeo Sant'Agata (page does not exist)") races.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-ARRS-4)

In 2009, an injury prevented him from competing for six 6 months, but he resolved the problem by working in the gym, together with a limited amount of running. He also improved his running posture and began the 2010 season with a view to competing in a [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon") in spring. After his debut in the [Prague Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prague_Marathon "Prague Marathon") (where he ran a time of 2:09:09 hours) and a win at the [Paris Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Half_Marathon "Paris Half Marathon"),[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-5) Kiprop turned to at the 10,000 m. His victory over the distance at the Kenyan Championships was unexpected, and his time (27:26.93) bettered the world best performance at altitude by almost 18 seconds. After that performance, Wilson was selected for the [African Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_African_Championships_in_Athletics "2010 African Championships in Athletics") in [Nairobi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi "Nairobi"), where he won in the 10,000 m [gold medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_medal "Gold medal"), beating [Moses Ndiema Kipsiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moses_Ndiema_Kipsiro "Moses Ndiema Kipsiro").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-6)

After a victory in [Lille Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lille_Half_Marathon "Lille Half Marathon") in September with his best time of 59:34,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-7) he focused his preparation towards the [2010 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "2010 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships") in [Nanning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanning "Nanning"). He defeated the defending champion, [Zersenay Tadese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zersenay_Tadese "Zersenay Tadese"), breaking his four-year unbeaten streak at the event.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-9)

The following year he was selected for the 10,000 m at the [2011 World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2011 World Championships in Athletics"), but had to withdraw due to injury.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-10) He returned to action in November, winning at the [Tuskys Wareng Cross Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuskys_Wareng_Cross_Country "Tuskys Wareng Cross Country").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-11) He closed the year with an appearance at the [BOClassic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BOClassic "BOClassic") 10K and he narrowly finished second to [Edwin Soi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Soi "Edwin Soi").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-12)

He defeated marathoner [Geoffrey Mutai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoffrey_Mutai "Geoffrey Mutai") to win the [Discovery Kenya Cross Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_Kenya_Cross_Country?action=edit&redlink=1 "Discovery Kenya Cross Country (page does not exist)") at the start of 2012.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-13) Despite being the pre-race favourite for the [Berlin Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Half_Marathon "Berlin Half Marathon"), he was beaten into second place by the lesser-known [Denis Koech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denis_Koech "Denis Koech"), although he ran a personal best time of 59:15 minutes.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-14) He secured his first place on the Kenyan Olympic team at the 2012 [Prefontaine Classic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prefontaine_Classic "Prefontaine Classic"), winning the 10,000 m trial race with a personal best of 27:01.98 minutes.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-15) Despite this strong performance, he failed to finish the distance when it came to the [2012 Olympic 10,000 metres final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2012_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_10,000_metres "Athletics at the 2012 Summer Olympics – Men's 10,000 metres").

In his first race of 2013, he won the [Roma-Ostia Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roma-Ostia_Half_Marathon "Roma-Ostia Half Marathon"), equalling his best of 59:15 minutes.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-16) He had a poor showing at the [Hamburg Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamburg_Marathon "Hamburg Marathon"), coming fifteenth in 2:19:20 hours, then failed to finish at the Kenyan 10,000 m trials.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-17) He won July's [Giro di Castelbuono](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giro_di_Castelbuono "Giro di Castelbuono") 10K, narrowly edging [Atanaw Ayalew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atanaw_Ayalew?action=edit&redlink=1 "Atanaw Ayalew (page does not exist)") at the line.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-18) He failed to finish the 10,000 m Kenyan Trials and missed the [2013 World Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2013 World Championships in Athletics") as a result. Instead he focused on the road and won the [Portugal Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portugal_Half_Marathon "Portugal Half Marathon") in October with a course record of 1:00:19 hours.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-19) He was in the top three at the [Giro al Sas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giro_al_Sas "Giro al Sas"), [BOclassic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BOclassic "BOclassic") and [Delhi Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delhi_Half_Marathon "Delhi Half Marathon") that year.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-21)

He began 2014 with his second career win at the Discovery Kenya Cross.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-22)

After a victory in [Lille Half Marathon](link_26) in September with his best time of 59:34,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-7) he focused his preparation towards the [2010 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships](link_7) in [Nanning](link_27). He defeated the defending champion, [Zersenay Tadese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zersenay_Tadese "Zersenay Tadese"), breaking his four-year unbeaten streak at the event.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-9)

The following year he was selected for the 10,000 m at the [2011 World Championships](link_28), but had to withdraw due to injury.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-10) He returned to action in November, winning at the [Tuskys Wareng Cross Country](link_29).[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-11) He closed the year with an appearance at the [BOClassic](link_30) 10K and he narrowly finished second to [Edwin Soi](link_31).[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-12)

He defeated marathoner [Geoffrey Mutai](link_32) to win the [Discovery Kenya Cross Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_Kenya_Cross_Country?action=edit&redlink=1 "Discovery Kenya Cross Country (page does not exist)") at the start of 2012.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-13) Despite being the pre-race favourite for the [Berlin Half Marathon](link_34), he was beaten into second place by the lesser-known [Denis Koech](link_35), although he ran a personal best time of 59:15 minutes.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-14) He secured his first place on the Kenyan Olympic team at the 2012 [Prefontaine Classic](link_36), winning the 10,000 m trial race with a personal best of 27:01.98 minutes.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-15) Despite this strong performance, he failed to finish the distance when it came to the [2012 Olympic 10,000 metres final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2012_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men [link_37]'s_10,000_metres "Athletics at the 2012 Summer Olympics – Men's 10,000 metres").

In his first race of 2013, he won the [Roma-Ostia Half Marathon](link_38), equalling his best of 59:15 minutes.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-16) He had a poor showing at the [Hamburg Marathon](link_39), coming fifteenth in 2:19:20 hours, then failed to finish at the Kenyan 10,000 m trials.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-17) He won July's [Giro di Castelbuono](link_40) 10K, narrowly edging [Atanaw Ayalew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atanaw_Ayalew?action=edit&redlink=1 "Atanaw Ayalew (page does not exist)") at the line.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-18) He failed to finish the 10,000 m Kenyan Trials and missed the [2013 World Championships in Athletics](link_41) as a result. Instead he focused on the road and won the [Portugal Half Marathon](link_42) in October with a course record of 1:00:19 hours.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-19) He was in the top three at the [Giro al Sas](link_43), [BOclassic](link_44) and [Delhi Half Marathon](link_45) that year.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-21)

He began 2014 with his second career win at the Discovery Kenya Cross.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-22)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Kenyan runner

**Benson Masya** (May 14, 1970 – September 24, 2003) was a Kenyan [long-distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_runner "Long-distance runner") and [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon") specialist, who competed in the late 1980s and 1990s. He participated at the inaugural [IAAF World Half Marathon Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "IAAF World Half Marathon Championships") in 1992 and finished in first place.

## Overview

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Benson_Masya&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Overview")]

Masya was a [Kamba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamba_people "Kamba people") by ethnicity.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benson_Masya#cite_note-1)

Initially he was a [boxer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boxing "Boxing") attached to Kenyan postal service before concentrating on running.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benson_Masya#cite_note-2) He won the [Great North Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_North_Run "Great North Run") a record four times; in 1991, 1992, 1994 and 1996. He also won the [City-Pier-City Loop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City-Pier-City_Loop "City-Pier-City Loop") half marathon in [the Hague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hague "The Hague") twice in 1993 and 1994.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benson_Masya#cite_note-3)

His career as a top runner came to a premature end. The Portsmouth 10 Mile race in 1996 was among his last notable achievements. His reveller lifestyle may have contributed to deteriorating performances.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benson_Masya#cite_note-4)

## Death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Benson_Masya&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Death")]

Masya died in September 2003, aged 33, after a period of illness. At his death, he was accompanied by his friend [Cosmas Ndeti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmas_Ndeti "Cosmas Ndeti"). Masya was buried in [Kitui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kitui "Kitui").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benson_Masya#cite_note-5)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Kenyan runner

**Benson Masya** (May 14, 1970 – September 24, 2003) was a Kenyan [long-distance runner](link_2) and [marathon](link_3) specialist, who competed in the late 1980s and 1990s. He participated at the inaugural [IAAF World Half Marathon Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "IAAF World Half Marathon Championships") in 1992 and finished in first place.

## Overview

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Benson_Masya&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Overview")]

Masya was a [Kamba](link_4) by ethnicity.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benson_Masya#cite_note-1)

Initially he was a [boxer](link_5) attached to Kenyan postal service before concentrating on running.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benson_Masya#cite_note-2) He won the [Great North Run](link_6) a record four times; in 1991, 1992, 1994 and 1996. He also won the [City-Pier-City Loop](link_7) half marathon in [the Hague](link_8) twice in 1993 and 1994.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benson_Masya#cite_note-3)

His career as a top runner came to a premature end. The Portsmouth 10 Mile race in 1996 was among his last notable achievements. His reveller lifestyle may have contributed to deteriorating performances.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benson_Masya#cite_note-4)

## Death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Benson_Masya&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Death")]

Masya died in September 2003, aged 33, after a period of illness. At his death, he was accompanied by his friend [Cosmas Ndeti](link_9). Masya was buried in [Kitui](link_10).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benson_Masya#cite_note-5)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Kenyan long-distance runner

[![Image 6](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/ff/Paul_kirui_amsterdam2007.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Paul_kirui_amsterdam2007.jpg)

Paul Kirui during the [Amsterdam Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam_Marathon "Amsterdam Marathon") 2007, where he finished fourth in 2:07:10.

**Paul Kiprop Kirui** (born February 5, 1980) is a [Kenyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenyan "Kenyan") distance and [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon")[runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Running "Running"). He participated at the [IAAF World Half Marathon Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "IAAF World Half Marathon Championships") in 2004 and finished first place. He had participated the World Half Marathon Championships twice before; in 2002 he finished 10th, but the next year he did not finish. His marathon personal best is 2:06:44, set in 2006 [Rotterdam Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotterdam_Marathon "Rotterdam Marathon"), when he finished 2nd behind compatriot [Sammy Korir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammy_Korir "Sammy Korir").

Kirui reached the podium at the 2010 [Seoul International Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seoul_International_Marathon "Seoul International Marathon"), taking third in 2:07:35 – his quickest time in three years.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kirui#cite_note-1)

*   2006 [Rotterdam Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotterdam_Marathon "Rotterdam Marathon") - 2nd (time 2:06:44, PB)

*   2009 [Rome Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome_Marathon "Rome Marathon") - 2nd [[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kirui#cite_note-2)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Kenyan long-distance runner

[![Image 6](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/ff/Paul_kirui_amsterdam2007.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Paul_kirui_amsterdam2007.jpg)

Paul Kirui during the [Amsterdam Marathon](link_2) 2007, where he finished fourth in 2:07:10.

**Paul Kiprop Kirui** (born February 5, 1980) is a [Kenyan](link_3) distance and [marathon](link_4)[runner](link_5). He participated at the [IAAF World Half Marathon Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "IAAF World Half Marathon Championships") in 2004 and finished first place. He had participated the World Half Marathon Championships twice before; in 2002 he finished 10th, but the next year he did not finish. His marathon personal best is 2:06:44, set in 2006 [Rotterdam Marathon](link_7), when he finished 2nd behind compatriot [Sammy Korir](link_8).

Kirui reached the podium at the 2010 [Seoul International Marathon](link_9), taking third in 2:07:35 – his quickest time in three years.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kirui#cite_note-1)

## Marathon record

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paul_Kirui&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Marathon record")]

*   2005 [Venice Marathon](link_10) - 5th
*   2005 [Milan Marathon](link_11) - 2nd
*   2006 [Rotterdam Marathon](link_7) - 2nd (time 2:06:44, PB)
*   2006 [JoongAng Seoul Marathon](link_12) - 2nd
*   2008 [Rotterdam Marathon](link_7) - 5th
*   2008 [Amsterdam Marathon](link_2) - **1st**
*   2009 [Rome Marathon](link_13) - 2nd [[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kirui#cite_note-2)

## Half marathon record

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paul_Kirui&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Half marathon record")]

*   [2002 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships](link_14) ([Brussels](link_15), BEL) - 1st
*   2003 [Berlin Half Marathon](link_16) - **1st**.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kirui#cite_note-3)
*   [2003 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships](link_17) ([Vilamoura](link_18), POR) - DNF
*   2004 [Berlin Half Marathon](link_16) - **1st**
*   [2004 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships](link_19) ([New Delhi](link_20), IND) - **1st**

**Moses Tanui** (born 20 August 1965 in Sugoi, [Nandi District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nandi_District "Nandi District"), [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya")) is a former [Kenyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya")[long-distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_runner "Long-distance runner") who won the gold medal over [10,000m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000m "10,000m") at the [1991 World Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1991_World_Championships_in_Athletics "1991 World Championships in Athletics") in Tokyo.

## Biography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Moses_Tanui&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

At the [1993 World Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1993_World_Championships_in_Athletics "1993 World Championships in Athletics") in Stuttgart he finished second after a controversial incident on the final lap in which he lost one shoe after the eventual winner [Haile Gebrselassie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie "Haile Gebrselassie") stepped repeatedly, lap after lap as a race video reveals, upon Tanui's heels. He also won the 100th [Boston Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Marathon "Boston Marathon") in 1996 as well as the 102nd Boston Marathon in 1998. Tanui won the [IAAF World Half Marathon Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "IAAF World Half Marathon Championships") in 1995 and silver in the 1997 competition.

He was the first athlete to run a [half marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon "Half marathon") in less than one hour by running 59:47 in [Milan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milan "Milan") on 3 April 1993. His record was broken five years later by fellow Kenyan [Paul Tergat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat "Paul Tergat").

At the [Chicago Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Marathon "Chicago Marathon") in 1999, Tanui helped spur [Khalid Khannouchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khalid_Khannouchi "Khalid Khannouchi") to a new world record, eventually finishing 2nd in 2:06:16, which was a Kenyan national record and the third fastest marathon in history at that point.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moses_Tanui#cite_note-1)

He was still active in 2004 when he competed at the [Seoul International Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seoul_International_Marathon "Seoul International Marathon"). He retired later due to a knee injury. Today he operates a training camp in [Kaptagat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaptagat "Kaptagat")[](https://web.archive.org/web/20070714031505/http://www.lornah.com/nieuws.htm). Tanui has also initiated two of Eldoret's most prominent events, the Discovery Cross Country race, and the Eldoret City Marathon.

He was involved in a serious car accident near [Nakuru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nakuru "Nakuru") in February 2010 suffering major injuries to his leg and chest. [David Lelei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Lelei "David Lelei"), another former runner, was driving Tanui's car and died in the accident.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moses_Tanui#cite_note-2)

**Moses Tanui** (born 20 August 1965 in Sugoi, [Nandi District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nandi_District "Nandi District"), [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya")) is a former [Kenyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya")[long-distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_runner "Long-distance runner") who won the gold medal over [10,000m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000m "10,000m") at the [1991 World Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1991_World_Championships_in_Athletics "1991 World Championships in Athletics") in Tokyo.

## Biography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Moses_Tanui&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

At the [1993 World Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1993_World_Championships_in_Athletics "1993 World Championships in Athletics") in Stuttgart he finished second after a controversial incident on the final lap in which he lost one shoe after the eventual winner [Haile Gebrselassie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie "Haile Gebrselassie") stepped repeatedly, lap after lap as a race video reveals, upon Tanui's heels. He also won the 100th [Boston Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Marathon "Boston Marathon") in 1996 as well as the 102nd Boston Marathon in 1998. Tanui won the [IAAF World Half Marathon Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "IAAF World Half Marathon Championships") in 1995 and silver in the 1997 competition.

He was the first athlete to run a [half marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon "Half marathon") in less than one hour by running 59:47 in [Milan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milan "Milan") on 3 April 1993. His record was broken five years later by fellow Kenyan [Paul Tergat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat "Paul Tergat").

At the [Chicago Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Marathon "Chicago Marathon") in 1999, Tanui helped spur [Khalid Khannouchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khalid_Khannouchi "Khalid Khannouchi") to a new world record, eventually finishing 2nd in 2:06:16, which was a Kenyan national record and the third fastest marathon in history at that point.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moses_Tanui#cite_note-1)

He was still active in 2004 when he competed at the [Seoul International Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seoul_International_Marathon "Seoul International Marathon"). He retired later due to a knee injury. Today he operates a training camp in [Kaptagat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaptagat "Kaptagat")[](https://web.archive.org/web/20070714031505/http://www.lornah.com/nieuws.htm). Tanui has also initiated two of Eldoret's most prominent events, the Discovery Cross Country race, and the Eldoret City Marathon.

He was involved in a serious car accident near [Nakuru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nakuru "Nakuru") in February 2010 suffering major injuries to his leg and chest. [David Lelei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Lelei "David Lelei"), another former runner, was driving Tanui's car and died in the accident.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moses_Tanui#cite_note-2)

Medal record Men's [athletics](link_6) Representing ![Image 3: Kenya](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/Flag_of_Kenya.svg/40px-Flag_of_Kenya.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)[Kenya](link_0) [World Half Marathon Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "IAAF World Half Marathon Championships") ![Image 4: Gold medal – first place](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d5/Gold_medal_icon_%28G_initial%29.svg/20px-Gold_medal_icon_%28G_initial%29.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)[2010 Nanning](link_7)Individual ![Image 5: Gold medal – first place](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d5/Gold_medal_icon_%28G_initial%29.svg/20px-Gold_medal_icon_%28G_initial%29.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)2010 Nanning Team [African Championships](link_8) ![Image 6: Gold medal – first place](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d5/Gold_medal_icon_%28G_initial%29.svg/20px-Gold_medal_icon_%28G_initial%29.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)[2010 Nairobi](link_9)[10,000 m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_African_Championships_in_Athletics_%E2%80%93_Men [link_10]'s_10,000_metres "2010 African Championships in Athletics – Men's 10,000 metres")

**Wilson Kiprop** (born 14 April 1987 in Soi, [Uasin Gishu District](link_11))[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-1) is a Kenyan [long-distance runner](link_1), who specialises in the [10,000 metres](link_12) and [half marathon](link_3). He was the world champion at the [IAAF World Half Marathon Championships](link_14) in 2010 and was the 10,000 m [gold medalist](link_15) at the [2010 African Championships in Athletics](link_9).

He started competing at the top level in 2008, winning competitions in Italy ([cross](link_16) and [road races](link_17)) and working under two Italian coaches, [Renato Canova](link_5) and Gabriele Nicola. He was the 2008 champion at the [Cross della Vallagarina](link_18) and the [Corrida di San Geminiano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corrida_di_San_Geminiano?action=edit&redlink=1 "Corrida di San Geminiano (page does not exist)").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-3) The following year he won the Vallagarina race for a second time running and came first at the [Eurocross](link_19) and [Trofeo Sant'Agata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trofeo_Sant [link_20]'Agata?action=edit&redlink=1 "Trofeo Sant'Agata (page does not exist)") races.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-ARRS-4)

In 2009, an injury prevented him from competing for six 6 months, but he resolved the problem by working in the gym, together with a limited amount of running. He also improved his running posture and began the 2010 season with a view to competing in a [marathon](link_4) in spring. After his debut in the [Prague Marathon](link_22) (where he ran a time of 2:09:09 hours) and a win at the [Paris Half Marathon](link_23),[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-5) Kiprop turned to at the 10,000 m. His victory over the distance at the Kenyan Championships was unexpected, and his time (27:26.93) bettered the world best performance at altitude by almost 18 seconds. After that performance, Wilson was selected for the [African Championships](link_9) in [Nairobi](link_24), where he won in the 10,000 m [gold medal](link_15), beating [Moses Ndiema Kipsiro](link_25).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-6)

After a victory in [Lille Half Marathon](link_26) in September with his best time of 59:34,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-7) he focused his preparation towards the [2010 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships](link_7) in [Nanning](link_27). He defeated the defending champion, [Zersenay Tadese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zersenay_Tadese "Zersenay Tadese"), breaking his four-year unbeaten streak at the event.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-9)

The following year he was selected for the 10,000 m at the [2011 World Championships](link_28), but had to withdraw due to injury.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-10) He returned to action in November, winning at the [Tuskys Wareng Cross Country](link_29).[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-11) He closed the year with an appearance at the [BOClassic](link_30) 10K and he narrowly finished second to [Edwin Soi](link_31).[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-12)

He defeated marathoner [Geoffrey Mutai](link_32) to win the [Discovery Kenya Cross Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_Kenya_Cross_Country?action=edit&redlink=1 "Discovery Kenya Cross Country (page does not exist)") at the start of 2012.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-13) Despite being the pre-race favourite for the [Berlin Half Marathon](link_34), he was beaten into second place by the lesser-known [Denis Koech](link_35), although he ran a personal best time of 59:15 minutes.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-14) He secured his first place on the Kenyan Olympic team at the 2012 [Prefontaine Classic](link_36), winning the 10,000 m trial race with a personal best of 27:01.98 minutes.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-15) Despite this strong performance, he failed to finish the distance when it came to the [2012 Olympic 10,000 metres final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2012_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men [link_37]'s_10,000_metres "Athletics at the 2012 Summer Olympics – Men's 10,000 metres").

In his first race of 2013, he won the [Roma-Ostia Half Marathon](link_38), equalling his best of 59:15 minutes.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-16) He had a poor showing at the [Hamburg Marathon](link_39), coming fifteenth in 2:19:20 hours, then failed to finish at the Kenyan 10,000 m trials.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-17) He won July's [Giro di Castelbuono](link_40) 10K, narrowly edging [Atanaw Ayalew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atanaw_Ayalew?action=edit&redlink=1 "Atanaw Ayalew (page does not exist)") at the line.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-18) He failed to finish the 10,000 m Kenyan Trials and missed the [2013 World Championships in Athletics](link_41) as a result. Instead he focused on the road and won the [Portugal Half Marathon](link_42) in October with a course record of 1:00:19 hours.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-19) He was in the top three at the [Giro al Sas](link_43), [BOclassic](link_44) and [Delhi Half Marathon](link_45) that year.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-21)

He began 2014 with his second career win at the Discovery Kenya Cross.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kiprop#cite_note-22)

**Stefano Baldini** (born 25 May 1971 in [Castelnovo di Sotto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castelnovo_di_Sotto "Castelnovo di Sotto"), [Emilia-Romagna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emilia-Romagna "Emilia-Romagna"), [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy")) is a retired [Italian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy")[runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_(sport) "Athletics (sport)") who specialized in the [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon"). He was the Olympic champion in [Athens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Summer_Olympics "2004 Summer Olympics") in 2004 and was twice European champion (1998 and 2006).

## Biography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stefano_Baldini&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

Baldini was also a world champion in the [half marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon "Half marathon"), taking the title in [Palma de Mallorca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "1996 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships") in 1996. In the [2004 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Summer_Olympics "2004 Summer Olympics"), Baldini finished first in the men's marathon, winning a gold medal. He finished ahead of Brazilian [Vanderlei de Lima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanderlei_de_Lima "Vanderlei de Lima"), who was leading the marathon until being pushed off the course by protester [Neil Horan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Horan "Neil Horan").

After a disappointing 2007 season in which he did not complete the London Marathon, Baldini chose to run the New York City Marathon, finishing 4th. Baldini closed his Olympic career at the [2008 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Summer_Olympics "2008 Summer Olympics"), finishing 12th.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stefano_Baldini#cite_note-2)

Baldini ended his career in October 2010, having originally planned a final race at the [Giro al Sas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giro_al_Sas "Giro al Sas") but deciding against the race because of injury.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stefano_Baldini#cite_note-3)

**William Henry Rodgers** (born December 23, 1947) is an American runner, Olympian, and former record holder in the [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon"). Rodgers is best known for his four victories in both the [Boston Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Marathon "Boston Marathon"), including three straight from 1978 to 1980, and 4 straight wins in the [New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Marathon "New York City Marathon"), between 1976 and 1979.

Born in [Hartford, Connecticut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartford,_Connecticut "Hartford, Connecticut"), Rodgers moved to [Newington, Connecticut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newington,_Connecticut "Newington, Connecticut"), with his family when he was around five. He attended [Newington High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newington_High_School "Newington High School"), where he played hockey and baseball, along with his older brother Charlie. When Newington High School added cross country as a sport in the fall of 1963, sophomore Bill Rodgers decided to join. Running track and cross country under coach Frank O'Rourke, Rodgers ran the mile in 4:28:8, won the 1965 Connecticut state cross country title and finished seventh in the New England Cross Country Championships.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Rodgers_(runner)#cite_note-auto-3) He first ran a road race at the Manchester Thanksgiving Day 4.78 mile race in 1965. Despite his amazing success, he never won this famous race.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Rodgers_(runner)#cite_note-4)

In the fall of 1966, Rodgers enrolled at [Wesleyan University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wesleyan_University "Wesleyan University") where he ran cross country and track, graduating with a B.A. in sociology in 1970. One of his teammates and college roommate, [Amby Burfoot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amby_Burfoot "Amby Burfoot"), won the 1968 [Boston Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Marathon "Boston Marathon") while still a student at Wesleyan and went on to edit _[Runner's World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runner's\_World "Runner's World")_ magazine. Another teammate and friend was future Olympian [Jeff Galloway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Galloway "Jeff Galloway"), who is a noted author on running.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Rodgers_(runner)#cite_note-auto-3)

After graduating in 1970, Rodgers enrolled to study and eventually receive his MS in special education from [Boston College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_College "Boston College"). After stepping away from competitive running for a time, in 1973, track coach [Bill Squires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Squires "Bill Squires") first formed the [Greater Boston Track Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Boston_Track_Club "Greater Boston Track Club") at Boston College to train small group of local elite runners, with Rodgers becoming one of them.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Rodgers_(runner)#cite_note-auto-3)

In April 1973, Rodgers entered his first [Boston Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Marathon "Boston Marathon"), dropping out at mile 20. After the race, Rodgers quit running for three months, only to return to training. Rodgers then won the Bay State Marathon in 2:28 in October 1973.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Rodgers_(runner)#cite_note-auto-3)

In April 1974, Rodgers returned to run the Boston Marathon, finishing 14th. On October 29, 1974, Rodgers ran his first [New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Marathon "New York City Marathon"), finishing fifth. One month after New York, Rodgers won the [Philadelphia Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia_Marathon "Philadelphia Marathon") in 2:21.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Rodgers_(runner)#cite_note-auto-3)

In 1975, Rodgers then burst into national prominence when he won the [1975 Boston Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1975_Boston_Marathon "1975 Boston Marathon") in 2:09:55, setting a new American record.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Rodgers_(runner)#cite_note-auto-3)

Rodgers won both the New York City Marathon and the Boston Marathon four times each between 1975 and 1980, twice breaking the American record at Boston with a time of 2:09:55 in 1975 and 2:09:27 in 1979. In 1977, he won the [Fukuoka Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fukuoka_Marathon "Fukuoka Marathon"), making him the only runner ever to hold the championship of all three major marathons at the same time. He made the 1976 U.S. Olympic team and raced the marathon at the [Montreal Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreal_Olympics "Montreal Olympics") in 1976, finishing 40th in 2:25:14. He did not participate in the [Olympics in 1980](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_Summer_Olympics "1980 Summer Olympics") due to the [U.S. boycott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_Summer_Olympics_boycott "1980 Summer Olympics boycott") over the invasion of [Afghanistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghanistan "Afghanistan") by the [USSR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USSR "USSR").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Rodgers_(runner)#cite_note-r1-1)

In 1975, Rodgers won the bronze medal at the [IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "IAAF World Cross Country Championships"), equaling Tracy Smith's 1966 bronze in the International [Cross Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_Country_Running "Cross Country Running") Championships as the highest an American had ever finished in international cross country competition. Rodgers' most remarkable year on the road racing circuit came in 1978 when he won 27 of the 30 races he entered, including the Pepsi 10 km nationals (with a new world road 10 km best time of 28:36.3), the [Falmouth Road Race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falmouth_Road_Race "Falmouth Road Race"), and the Boston and New York City marathons. Rodgers is also the former world record holder for 25 kilometers as he broke [Pekka Päivärinta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pekka_P%C3%A4iv%C3%A4rinta "Pekka Päivärinta")'s world record with a time of 1:14.11.8 on a track at [West Valley College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Valley_College "West Valley College") in [Saratoga, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saratoga,_California "Saratoga, California"), in 1979.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Rodgers_(runner)#cite_note-r1-1)

_[Track & Field News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Track\_&\_Field\_News "Track & Field News")_ ranked Rodgers number one in the world in the marathon in 1975, 1977 and 1979.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Rodgers_(runner)#cite_note-r1-1) Of the 59 marathons Rodgers ran, 28 were run under 2:15. In all, he won 22 marathons in his career. He came to be referred to by sportswriters and others as "Boston Billy".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Rodgers_(runner)#cite_note-5)

Rodgers was inducted to the [National Track and Field Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Track_and_Field_Hall_of_Fame "National Track and Field Hall of Fame") on December 3, 1999, in ceremonies in Los Angeles. In 1998, Rodgers was inducted in the first round to the [National Distance Running Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Distance_Running_Hall_of_Fame "National Distance Running Hall of Fame") in [Utica, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utica,_New_York "Utica, New York").

Rodgers has run the [Bix 7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bix_7 "Bix 7") road race in [Davenport, Iowa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davenport,_Iowa "Davenport, Iowa"), every year since 1980, earning the local nickname "Bix Billy". A bronze statue of Rodgers and [Joan Benoit Samuelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_Benoit_Samuelson "Joan Benoit Samuelson") was erected near the Bix finish line in 2007.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Rodgers_(runner)#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Rodgers_(runner)#cite_note-7)

On April 20, 2015, [Patriots' Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patriots'_Day "Patriots' Day"), Rodgers was honored by the [Boston Red Sox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Red_Sox "Boston Red Sox") as he threw out the [ceremonial first pitch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceremonial_first_pitch "Ceremonial first pitch") at [Fenway Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fenway_Park "Fenway Park").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Rodgers_(runner)#cite_note-8)

_Bill Rodgers Running Center_ in [Faneuil Hall Marketplace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faneuil_Hall_Marketplace "Faneuil Hall Marketplace") in Boston was owned and operated by Bill and his brother Charlie. The family-run business operated from 1977 to 2013.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Rodgers_(runner)#cite_note-9) He lives in the small town of [Boxborough, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boxborough,_Massachusetts "Boxborough, Massachusetts"), and still participates in running-themed events.

Rodgers was named as a Grand Marshal for the [2025 Boston Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Boston_Marathon "2025 Boston Marathon"), alongside long-time friend and fellow Boston Marathon champion, [Bob Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Hall_(wheelchair_athlete) "Bob Hall (wheelchair athlete)"), a wheelchair athlete.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Rodgers_(runner)#cite_note-10)

**William Henry Rodgers** (born December 23, 1947) is an American runner, Olympian, and former record holder in the [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon"). Rodgers is best known for his four victories in both the [Boston Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Marathon "Boston Marathon"), including three straight from 1978 to 1980, and 4 straight wins in the [New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Marathon "New York City Marathon"), between 1976 and 1979.

Born in [Hartford, Connecticut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartford,_Connecticut "Hartford, Connecticut"), Rodgers moved to [Newington, Connecticut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newington,_Connecticut "Newington, Connecticut"), with his family when he was around five. He attended [Newington High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newington_High_School "Newington High School"), where he played hockey and baseball, along with his older brother Charlie. When Newington High School added cross country as a sport in the fall of 1963, sophomore Bill Rodgers decided to join. Running track and cross country under coach Frank O'Rourke, Rodgers ran the mile in 4:28:8, won the 1965 Connecticut state cross country title and finished seventh in the New England Cross Country Championships.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Rodgers_(runner)#cite_note-auto-3) He first ran a road race at the Manchester Thanksgiving Day 4.78 mile race in 1965. Despite his amazing success, he never won this famous race.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Rodgers_(runner)#cite_note-4)

In the fall of 1966, Rodgers enrolled at [Wesleyan University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wesleyan_University "Wesleyan University") where he ran cross country and track, graduating with a B.A. in sociology in 1970. One of his teammates and college roommate, [Amby Burfoot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amby_Burfoot "Amby Burfoot"), won the 1968 [Boston Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Marathon "Boston Marathon") while still a student at Wesleyan and went on to edit _[Runner's World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runner's\_World "Runner's World")_ magazine. Another teammate and friend was future Olympian [Jeff Galloway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Galloway "Jeff Galloway"), who is a noted author on running.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Rodgers_(runner)#cite_note-auto-3)

After graduating in 1970, Rodgers enrolled to study and eventually receive his MS in special education from [Boston College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_College "Boston College"). After stepping away from competitive running for a time, in 1973, track coach [Bill Squires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Squires "Bill Squires") first formed the [Greater Boston Track Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Boston_Track_Club "Greater Boston Track Club") at Boston College to train small group of local elite runners, with Rodgers becoming one of them.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Rodgers_(runner)#cite_note-auto-3)

In April 1973, Rodgers entered his first [Boston Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Marathon "Boston Marathon"), dropping out at mile 20. After the race, Rodgers quit running for three months, only to return to training. Rodgers then won the Bay State Marathon in 2:28 in October 1973.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Rodgers_(runner)#cite_note-auto-3)

In April 1974, Rodgers returned to run the Boston Marathon, finishing 14th. On October 29, 1974, Rodgers ran his first [New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Marathon "New York City Marathon"), finishing fifth. One month after New York, Rodgers won the [Philadelphia Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia_Marathon "Philadelphia Marathon") in 2:21.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Rodgers_(runner)#cite_note-auto-3)

In 1975, Rodgers then burst into national prominence when he won the [1975 Boston Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1975_Boston_Marathon "1975 Boston Marathon") in 2:09:55, setting a new American record.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Rodgers_(runner)#cite_note-auto-3)

Rodgers won both the New York City Marathon and the Boston Marathon four times each between 1975 and 1980, twice breaking the American record at Boston with a time of 2:09:55 in 1975 and 2:09:27 in 1979. In 1977, he won the [Fukuoka Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fukuoka_Marathon "Fukuoka Marathon"), making him the only runner ever to hold the championship of all three major marathons at the same time. He made the 1976 U.S. Olympic team and raced the marathon at the [Montreal Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreal_Olympics "Montreal Olympics") in 1976, finishing 40th in 2:25:14. He did not participate in the [Olympics in 1980](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_Summer_Olympics "1980 Summer Olympics") due to the [U.S. boycott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_Summer_Olympics_boycott "1980 Summer Olympics boycott") over the invasion of [Afghanistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghanistan "Afghanistan") by the [USSR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USSR "USSR").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Rodgers_(runner)#cite_note-r1-1)

In 1975, Rodgers won the bronze medal at the [IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "IAAF World Cross Country Championships"), equaling Tracy Smith's 1966 bronze in the International [Cross Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_Country_Running "Cross Country Running") Championships as the highest an American had ever finished in international cross country competition. Rodgers' most remarkable year on the road racing circuit came in 1978 when he won 27 of the 30 races he entered, including the Pepsi 10 km nationals (with a new world road 10 km best time of 28:36.3), the [Falmouth Road Race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falmouth_Road_Race "Falmouth Road Race"), and the Boston and New York City marathons. Rodgers is also the former world record holder for 25 kilometers as he broke [Pekka Päivärinta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pekka_P%C3%A4iv%C3%A4rinta "Pekka Päivärinta")'s world record with a time of 1:14.11.8 on a track at [West Valley College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Valley_College "West Valley College") in [Saratoga, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saratoga,_California "Saratoga, California"), in 1979.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Rodgers_(runner)#cite_note-r1-1)

_[Track & Field News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Track\_&\_Field\_News "Track & Field News")_ ranked Rodgers number one in the world in the marathon in 1975, 1977 and 1979.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Rodgers_(runner)#cite_note-r1-1) Of the 59 marathons Rodgers ran, 28 were run under 2:15. In all, he won 22 marathons in his career. He came to be referred to by sportswriters and others as "Boston Billy".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Rodgers_(runner)#cite_note-5)

Rodgers was inducted to the [National Track and Field Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Track_and_Field_Hall_of_Fame "National Track and Field Hall of Fame") on December 3, 1999, in ceremonies in Los Angeles. In 1998, Rodgers was inducted in the first round to the [National Distance Running Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Distance_Running_Hall_of_Fame "National Distance Running Hall of Fame") in [Utica, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utica,_New_York "Utica, New York").

Rodgers has run the [Bix 7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bix_7 "Bix 7") road race in [Davenport, Iowa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davenport,_Iowa "Davenport, Iowa"), every year since 1980, earning the local nickname "Bix Billy". A bronze statue of Rodgers and [Joan Benoit Samuelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_Benoit_Samuelson "Joan Benoit Samuelson") was erected near the Bix finish line in 2007.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Rodgers_(runner)#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Rodgers_(runner)#cite_note-7)

On April 20, 2015, [Patriots' Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patriots'_Day "Patriots' Day"), Rodgers was honored by the [Boston Red Sox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Red_Sox "Boston Red Sox") as he threw out the [ceremonial first pitch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceremonial_first_pitch "Ceremonial first pitch") at [Fenway Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fenway_Park "Fenway Park").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Rodgers_(runner)#cite_note-8)

_Bill Rodgers Running Center_ in [Faneuil Hall Marketplace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faneuil_Hall_Marketplace "Faneuil Hall Marketplace") in Boston was owned and operated by Bill and his brother Charlie. The family-run business operated from 1977 to 2013.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Rodgers_(runner)#cite_note-9) He lives in the small town of [Boxborough, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boxborough,_Massachusetts "Boxborough, Massachusetts"), and still participates in running-themed events.

Rodgers was named as a Grand Marshal for the [2025 Boston Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Boston_Marathon "2025 Boston Marathon"), alongside long-time friend and fellow Boston Marathon champion, [Bob Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Hall_(wheelchair_athlete) "Bob Hall (wheelchair athlete)"), a wheelchair athlete.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Rodgers_(runner)#cite_note-10)

**Jacob Kiplimo** (born 14 November 2000)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-2) is a Ugandan [long-distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_running "Long-distance running") and former world record holder in the [half marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon "Half marathon").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-:0-3) A four-time individual [World Cross Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics_Cross_Country_Championships "World Athletics Cross Country Championships") champion, he won the junior title in [2017](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "2017 IAAF World Cross Country Championships") and senior titles in [2023](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_World_Athletics_Cross_Country_Championships "2023 World Athletics Cross Country Championships"), [2024](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_World_Athletics_Cross_Country_Championships "2024 World Athletics Cross Country Championships") and [2026](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_World_Athletics_Cross_Country_Championships "2026 World Athletics Cross Country Championships"). He also won [10,000m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres "10,000 metres") bronze medals at the [2020 Tokyo Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2020_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the 2020 Summer Olympics") and the [2022 World Athletics Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_World_Athletics_Championships "2022 World Athletics Championships").

Kiplimo ran 56:42 at the 2025 [Barcelona Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barcelona_Half_Marathon "Barcelona Half Marathon"), but [World Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics "World Athletics") did not ratify the performance because of assistance from a lead pace car.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-WR_denied-4) He subsequently set a ratified half-marathon world record of 57:20 at the 2026 [Lisbon Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon_Half_Marathon "Lisbon Half Marathon").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-:0-3)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-5) His time of 2:00:28 at the [2026 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_London_Marathon "2026 London Marathon") makes him the third-fastest [marathoner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon") of all time.

Kiplimo was born on 14 November 2000.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-WAprofile-6) A member of the [Sebei ethnic group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sebei_people "Sebei people"), he grew up in [Kween](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kween_District "Kween District") on [Mount Elgon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Elgon "Mount Elgon"), living at a high altitude.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-Eagle-7) His family grew [maize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize "Maize"). As a young child, Kiplimo would watch his older brothers train for athletic events. He would also travel to school by running a distance of 5 km. Kiplimo won a selection trial for the [World Mountain Running Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Mountain_Running_Championships "World Mountain Running Championships") in 2015 but was not allowed to compete due to his age. Kiplimo then moved to Italy and began competing in events. After winning a 2017 cross country event in Uganda, he moved back.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-8)

At the age of fifteen, Kiplimo won the [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres "10,000 metres") bronze medal at the [2016 IAAF World U20 Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_IAAF_World_U20_Championships "2016 IAAF World U20 Championships") behind fellow East Africans [Rodgers Kwemoi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rodgers_Kwemoi "Rodgers Kwemoi") and [Aron Kifle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aron_Kifle "Aron Kifle"). He ran [5000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres") in [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome "Rome") that May at 13:24:40 minutes, which was a qualifying time for the Olympics. Kiplimo was then selected for [2016 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics "Uganda at the 2016 Summer Olympics").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-Eagle-7) Before the [2016 Rio Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the 2016 Summer Olympics"), he improved his 5000 m best to 13:19.54 minutes. As the youngest entrant to the competition, he ran in the Olympic heats only, recording a time of 13:30.40 minutes for 11th in his race.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-9) He was the youngest ever competitor for Uganda at the Olympic Games.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-11)

At 16, Kiplimo won gold in the men's U20 race at the [2017 World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "2017 IAAF World Cross Country Championships") in [Kampala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kampala "Kampala"), the country's first-ever gold medal at a World Cross, covering a 8 km course in 22:40 minutes.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-12) He won the [San Silvestre Vallecana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Silvestre_Vallecana "San Silvestre Vallecana")[10 km road race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run "10K run") in [Madrid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madrid "Madrid") in a time of 26:41 on 31 December 2018. The course had an elevation drop, making it ineligible for world record status.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-13)

At the Ugandan Cross Country Championships on 16 February in [Tororo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tororo "Tororo"), Kiplimo defeated [Joshua Cheptegei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei "Joshua Cheptegei") by placing first and second, respectively. In the men's senior race over 10 km, Kiplimo won by an 11-second lead over the 10,000 m world championship runner-up.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-14)

At the [World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "2019 IAAF World Cross Country Championships") in [Aarhus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aarhus "Aarhus"), Denmark, Kiplimo finished second in the senior men's race four seconds after [Joshua Cheptegei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei "Joshua Cheptegei")'s winning time of 31:40. He won the gold medal in the teams ranking with Cheptegei from Uganda.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-15)

Kiplimo did not run in the 10,000 metres at the [World Athletics Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_World_Athletics_Championships "2019 World Athletics Championships") in [Doha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doha "Doha") because of an injury.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-17)

On 31 December, Kiplimo ran the [Saint Silvester Road Race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Silvester_Road_Race "Saint Silvester Road Race") (15 km) in [São Paulo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Paulo "São Paulo") and was beaten by [Kibiwott Kandie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kibiwott_Kandie "Kibiwott Kandie") at the finish line. Kandie won in 42:59, a new course record, with Kiplimo finishing in 43:00.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-18)

On 8 September, Kiplimo won the 5000 m run in [Ostrava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ostrava "Ostrava"), Czech Republic in a time of 12:48.63 and improved his personal best of 13:13.64 set as a 16-year-old at the 2017 [Prefontaine Classic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prefontaine_Classic "Prefontaine Classic"). [Selemon Barega](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selemon_Barega "Selemon Barega") was the runner up with a time 12:49.08, while his personal best of 12:43.02 was the fifth-fastest ever at the time.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-19) On 17 September, Kiplimo won a [Diamond League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Diamond_League "2020 Diamond League") 3000 m run in [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome "Rome") with a time of 7:26.64.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-20) Kiplimo won the [Half Marathon World Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "2020 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships") in a time of 58:49 on 17 October in [Gdynia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gdynia "Gdynia"), Poland. His time was a Ugandan record and championship record.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-21)

On 6 December, he competed in the [Valencia Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valencia_Half_Marathon "Valencia Half Marathon") against [Kibiwott Kandie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kibiwott_Kandie "Kibiwott Kandie"), [Rhonex Kipruto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhonex_Kipruto "Rhonex Kipruto"), and [Alexander Mutiso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Mutiso "Alexander Mutiso"). They all broke the previous world record of 58:01, set by [Geoffrey Kamworor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoffrey_Kamworor "Geoffrey Kamworor") in 2019. Kandie set the new world record time at 57:32. Kiplimo placed second in the race with a time of 57:37.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-22)

On 21 March 2021, Kiplimo competed at the [Campaccio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campaccio "Campaccio") cross country race in [San Giorgio su Legnano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Giorgio_su_Legnano "San Giorgio su Legnano"), Italy. Despite falling during the ninth kilometer of the race, he won a 10 km in 29:07. Ethiopia's [Nibret Melak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nibret_Melak "Nibret Melak") finished second, and Kiplimo's younger brother [Oscar Chelimo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oscar_Chelimo "Oscar Chelimo") finished third.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-23) On 19 May, Kiplimo returned to the track racing 10,000 m at the 60th [Ostrava Golden Spike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ostrava_Golden_Spike "Ostrava Golden Spike"). He pulled away from Bahrain's [Birhanu Balew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birhanu_Balew "Birhanu Balew") to win the race. Kiplimo finished in a personal best time of 26:33.93, which made him the seventh-fastest 10,000 m performer of all time and the second-fastest Ugandan in history over the distance behind world record holder [Joshua Cheptegei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei "Joshua Cheptegei")'s 26:11.00.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-24)

On 21 November 2021, Kiplimo set a half marathon world record at 57:31 in Lisbon.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-25) His record was broken by [Yomif Kejelcha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yomif_Kejelcha "Yomif Kejelcha"), who ran a time of 57:30 at the [2024 Valencia Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valencia_Half_Marathon "Valencia Half Marathon").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-26)

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b0/Jacob_Kiplimo_at_the_2025_Chicago_Marathon.jpg/250px-Jacob_Kiplimo_at_the_2025_Chicago_Marathon.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jacob_Kiplimo_at_the_2025_Chicago_Marathon.jpg)

Jacob Kiplimo one mile before winning the 2025 Chicago Marathon.

On 18 February, Kiplimo won the gold medal in the 10-kilometer race at the [World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_World_Athletics_Cross_Country_Championships "2023 World Athletics Cross Country Championships") held in [Bathurst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bathurst,_New_South_Wales "Bathurst, New South Wales"), Australia with a time of 29:17. Ethiopian [Berihu Aregawi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berihu_Aregawi "Berihu Aregawi") finished second in 29:26 followed by [Joshua Cheptegei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei "Joshua Cheptegei") (29:37), world record holder for the 5000 m and 10,000 m, who had been defending his title from [Aarhus 2019](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "2019 IAAF World Cross Country Championships").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-27)

On 16 February, Kiplimo regained the world record in the half marathon, finishing the [Barcelona Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barcelona_Half_Marathon "Barcelona Half Marathon") in 56 minutes and 42 seconds.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-28) On 5 February 2026, that record was stripped by World Athletics because it is suspected that the lead car of the race offered Kiplimo a "pacing advantage".[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-29) Barcelona Half Marathon race direction later stated that they will appeal this decision.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-30)

On 27 April, Kiplimo made his marathon debut at the 2025 London Marathon, finishing in second behind Sabastian Sawe with a time of 2:03:37, a Ugandan national record.

On 12 October, Kiplimo won the 2025 Chicago Marathon, finishing in 2:02:23 and marking his first marathon win.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-31)

On 8 March, Kiplimo returned to the EDP Lisbon Half Marathon and retook the half marathon world record at 57:20.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-32)

On 26 April, Kiplimo ran the third-fastest marathon in history at the [2026 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_London_Marathon "2026 London Marathon"), finishing in 2:00:28. The race also saw [Sabastian Sawe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sabastian_Sawe "Sabastian Sawe") and [Yomif Kejelcha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yomif_Kejelcha "Yomif Kejelcha") finish in 1:59:30 and 1:59:41, respectively, all three surpassing the previous world record of 2:00:35 set by Kelvin Kiptum.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-33)
