**Vincent Rousseau** (born 29 July 1962 in [Mons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mons,_Belgium "Mons, Belgium"), [Hainaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hainaut_(province) "Hainaut (province)")) is a Belgian former [long-distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_runner "Long-distance runner"), who competed in three consecutive [Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer_Olympics "Summer Olympics") for his native country, starting in 1984.

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vincent_Rousseau&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Career")]

In 1993, he had his biggest success by winning the [IAAF World Half Marathon Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "IAAF World Half Marathon Championships") in [Brussels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brussels "Brussels"), the next year followed by the first place in the [Rotterdam Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotterdam_Marathon "Rotterdam Marathon").

He had much success at the [Lotto Cross Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lotto_Cross_Cup "Lotto Cross Cup") (Belgium's annual [cross country running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_country_running "Cross country running") series) and was the overall season winner five times consecutively between 1983–88 and he earned a further three consecutive wins between 1990 and 1993.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_Rousseau#cite_note-1)

Among his other wins on the circuit were the [Dam tot Damloop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dam_tot_Damloop "Dam tot Damloop") in 1987, [Eurocross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurocross "Eurocross") in 1990,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_Rousseau#cite_note-2) and the [20 km of Brussels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/20_km_of_Brussels "20 km of Brussels") in 1995.

## Awards

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vincent_Rousseau&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Awards")]

Rousseau was twice named [Belgian Sportsman of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgian_Sportsman_of_the_year "Belgian Sportsman of the year") in 1985 and 1993.

He won the [Belgian National Sports Merit Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgian_National_Sports_Merit_Award "Belgian National Sports Merit Award") in 1993.

**Vincent Rousseau** (born 29 July 1962 in [Mons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mons,_Belgium "Mons, Belgium"), [Hainaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hainaut_(province) "Hainaut (province)")) is a Belgian former [long-distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_runner "Long-distance runner"), who competed in three consecutive [Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer_Olympics "Summer Olympics") for his native country, starting in 1984.

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vincent_Rousseau&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Career")]

In 1993, he had his biggest success by winning the [IAAF World Half Marathon Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "IAAF World Half Marathon Championships") in [Brussels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brussels "Brussels"), the next year followed by the first place in the [Rotterdam Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotterdam_Marathon "Rotterdam Marathon").

He had much success at the [Lotto Cross Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lotto_Cross_Cup "Lotto Cross Cup") (Belgium's annual [cross country running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_country_running "Cross country running") series) and was the overall season winner five times consecutively between 1983–88 and he earned a further three consecutive wins between 1990 and 1993.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_Rousseau#cite_note-1)

Among his other wins on the circuit were the [Dam tot Damloop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dam_tot_Damloop "Dam tot Damloop") in 1987, [Eurocross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurocross "Eurocross") in 1990,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_Rousseau#cite_note-2) and the [20 km of Brussels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/20_km_of_Brussels "20 km of Brussels") in 1995.

## Awards

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vincent_Rousseau&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Awards")]

Rousseau was twice named [Belgian Sportsman of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgian_Sportsman_of_the_year "Belgian Sportsman of the year") in 1985 and 1993.

He won the [Belgian National Sports Merit Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgian_National_Sports_Merit_Award "Belgian National Sports Merit Award") in 1993.

**Shem Kororia** (born 25 September 1972) is a former [Kenyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya") long-distance runner who specialized in the [5000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres") and [half marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon "Half marathon"). He represented his native country at the [1996 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_Summer_Olympics "1996 Summer Olympics") in [Atlanta, United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta,_United_States "Atlanta, United States"). Kororia was the third man ever to run the half marathon within an hour, when he won the [world half marathon title](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "1997 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships") in October 1997 in [Košice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ko%C5%A1ice "Košice"), [Slovakia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia "Slovakia"), clocking 59:56 minutes.

He won 5000 metres gold twice at the [Military World Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_World_Games "Military World Games"): in 1995 and 1999.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shem_Kororia#cite_note-1) He also won the [Parelloop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parelloop "Parelloop") 10K in race in the [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands") in 1997 and had back-to-back wins at the [BOclassic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BOclassic "BOclassic") in 1994–95.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shem_Kororia#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shem_Kororia#cite_note-3)

He also competed in [cross country running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_country_running "Cross country running") events. He was twice a team gold medallist with Kenya at the [IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "IAAF World Cross Country Championships") ([1994](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1994_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "1994 IAAF World Cross Country Championships") and [1997](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "1997 IAAF World Cross Country Championships")). On the major cross country meet circuit he had two wins at the [Cross Internacional de la Constitución](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_Internacional_de_la_Constituci%C3%B3n "Cross Internacional de la Constitución") (1994 and 1995) and was the 1996 winner of both the [Campaccio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campaccio "Campaccio") and the [Cross Internacional de Venta de Baños](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_Internacional_de_Venta_de_Ba%C3%B1os "Cross Internacional de Venta de Baños") races.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shem_Kororia#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shem_Kororia#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shem_Kororia#cite_note-6)

He is from [Kaptama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaptama "Kaptama") in [Mount Elgon District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Elgon_District "Mount Elgon District"), the same village as [Edith Masai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edith_Masai "Edith Masai").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shem_Kororia#cite_note-7)

Kororia was the third man ever to run the half marathon within an hour, when he won the [world half marathon title](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "1997 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships") in October 1997 in [Košice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ko%C5%A1ice "Košice"), [Slovakia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia "Slovakia"), clocking 59:56 minutes.

He won 5000 metres gold twice at the [Military World Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_World_Games "Military World Games"): in 1995 and 1999.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shem_Kororia#cite_note-1) He also won the [Parelloop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parelloop "Parelloop") 10K in race in the [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands") in 1997 and had back-to-back wins at the [BOclassic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BOclassic "BOclassic") in 1994–95.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shem_Kororia#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shem_Kororia#cite_note-3)

He also competed in [cross country running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_country_running "Cross country running") events. He was twice a team gold medallist with Kenya at the [IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "IAAF World Cross Country Championships") ([1994](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1994_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "1994 IAAF World Cross Country Championships") and [1997](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "1997 IAAF World Cross Country Championships")). On the major cross country meet circuit he had two wins at the [Cross Internacional de la Constitución](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_Internacional_de_la_Constituci%C3%B3n "Cross Internacional de la Constitución") (1994 and 1995) and was the 1996 winner of both the [Campaccio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campaccio "Campaccio") and the [Cross Internacional de Venta de Baños](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_Internacional_de_Venta_de_Ba%C3%B1os "Cross Internacional de Venta de Baños") races.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shem_Kororia#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shem_Kororia#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shem_Kororia#cite_note-6)

He is from [Kaptama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaptama "Kaptama") in [Mount Elgon District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Elgon_District "Mount Elgon District"), the same village as [Edith Masai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edith_Masai "Edith Masai").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shem_Kororia#cite_note-7)

**Paul Malakwen Kosgei** (born 22 April 1978, in [Marakwet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marakwet "Marakwet")) is a Kenyan [long-distance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_running "Long-distance running") and [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon_race "Marathon race") runner. He first came to prominence in athletics by taking the World Junior Record of 3000m steeple in 1997, and later with consecutive medals at the [IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "IAAF World Cross Country Championships") from 1998 to 2000.

In 1999 he started his technical collaboration with the Italian Coach Renato Canova, that changed his event, looking at longer distances.

He made his debut at the [IAAF World Half Marathon Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "IAAF World Half Marathon Championships") in 2002 and became the surprise world champion for the event. Later that year he became the African champion on the track in the [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres "10,000 metres") and also won [silver medals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_medal "Silver medal") at the [2002 Commonwealth Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Commonwealth_Games "2002 Commonwealth Games") and [2002 IAAF World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_IAAF_World_Cup "2002 IAAF World Cup").

He focused entirely on [road running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_running "Road running") after 2002 and he broke the [world record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_world_records_in_athletics "List of world records in athletics") for the 25 km distance, running 1:12:45 in May 2004. His personal best over the [half marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon "Half marathon") (59:07 minutes), with which he won the 2006 [Berlin Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Half_Marathon "Berlin Half Marathon"), ranks him within the top ten fastest ever over the distance.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei#cite_note-1) He began to focus on marathon running and won his first race at the [Maratona d'Italia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maratona_d'Italia "Maratona d'Italia") in 2010 with a course record and personal best time of 2:09.00.

From 2009 there was a passage of coach, from Renato Canova to Gabriele Nicola, who is a student of the former coach.

### Junior world record and first medals

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Junior world record and first medals")]

Kosgei started his international career as a [cross country runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_country_runner "Cross country runner") and a [steeplechaser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steeplechase_(athletics) "Steeplechase (athletics)"). He came to prominence as a junior athlete in 1997 when he took the junior [bronze medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronze_medal "Bronze medal") at the [1997 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "1997 IAAF World Cross Country Championships"), and he also reached the [1997 IAAF Grand Prix Final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_IAAF_Grand_Prix_Final "1997 IAAF Grand Prix Final") for the [3000 metres steeplechase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3000_metres_steeplechase "3000 metres steeplechase"). He established his pedigree by setting a [world junior record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_world_junior_records_in_athletics "List of world junior records in athletics") for the event.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei#cite_note-IAAFBio-2)

He emerged as a senior the following year, taking the bronze in the short race at the [1998 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "1998 IAAF World Cross Country Championships") and helping Kenya to the team [gold medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_medal "Gold medal").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei#cite_note-IAAFBio-2) He also led Kenya to a team victory at the [IAAF World Road Relay Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Road_Relay_Championships "IAAF World Road Relay Championships") in [Manaus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manaus "Manaus") in April.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei#cite_note-3) He was the fourth fastest athlete in the world that year in the steeplechase. He also began taking part in [road running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_running "Road running") competitions and won the 10 km [BOclassic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BOclassic "BOclassic") race at the end of the year.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei#cite_note-4) He improved to the [silver medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_medal "Silver medal") position at the [1999 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "1999 IAAF World Cross Country Championships"), finishing behind [Paul Tergat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat "Paul Tergat") to help Kenya to a consecutive team win. He represented his country on the track at the [1999 World Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_World_Championships_in_Athletics "1999 World Championships in Athletics") in [Seville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville "Seville"), where he was seventh in the men's steeplechase. He closed his track season with a fifth-place finish at the [1999 IAAF Grand Prix Final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_IAAF_Grand_Prix_Final "1999 IAAF Grand Prix Final").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei#cite_note-IAAFBio-2)

### African and World Champion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: African and World Champion")]

From 2000 onwards he later began concentrating on [long-distance running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_running "Long-distance running") and dropped his steeplechase speciality. He set a 10 km best of 27:40 to win the [Parelloop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parelloop "Parelloop") race in [Brunssum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brunssum "Brunssum") that year.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei#cite_note-5) He also took a third consecutive cross country medal at the [2000 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "2000 IAAF World Cross Country Championships"), continuing the streak of Kenya team victories with his bronze medal performance.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei#cite_note-IAAFBio-2) He took road circuit wins in Europe at the [Giro Podistico Internazionale di Pettinengo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giro_Podistico_Internazionale_di_Pettinengo?action=edit&redlink=1 "Giro Podistico Internazionale di Pettinengo (page does not exist)"), winning the 9.5 km race in 27:03,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei#cite_note-6) and also at the [Giro al Sas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giro_al_Sas "Giro al Sas") 10K in [Trento](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trento "Trento").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei#cite_note-7) He ran for Kenya in the long race at the [2001 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "2001 IAAF World Cross Country Championships") but could not match his short course form and finished in fifth place. The greater distances also did not bring him medals at the [2001 World Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2001 World Championships in Athletics") as he finished seventh in the [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres "10,000 metres") final.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei#cite_note-IAAFBio-2) He was the winner of the 2001 [Giro Media Blenio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giro_Media_Blenio "Giro Media Blenio") 10K race in [Dongio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dongio "Dongio"), recording a time of 28:13.4.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei#cite_note-8)

The 2002 marked a significant breakthrough for Kosgei in both track and road running. In May, he led the Kenyan team to victory at the [2002 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "2002 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships") with a time of 1:00:39. He edged out [Jaouad Gharib](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaouad_Gharib "Jaouad Gharib") to win the race on his first attempt at the [half marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon "Half marathon") distance. His first time success did not make him an immediate convert, however: "I have changed my focus from the steeplechase to the 10,000 metres ... Maybe in two or three years I will start to think about running the marathon".[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei#cite_note-9) Kosgei became the Kenyan champion over 10,000 m that summer,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei#cite_note-10) and his next test came at the [2002 Commonwealth Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2002_Commonwealth_Games "Athletics at the 2002 Commonwealth Games") in Manchester, England. He was entered into the 10,000 m race and was second behind his Kenyan compatriot [Wilberforce Talel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilberforce_Talel "Wilberforce Talel") – Kosgei's finishing time of 27:45.46 was seven hundredths of a second behind Talel, who broke the [Games record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Commonwealth_Games_records_in_athletics "List of Commonwealth Games records in athletics") for the event.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei#cite_note-11)

He went unbeaten over the distance at the [2002 African Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_African_Championships_in_Athletics "2002 African Championships in Athletics") the following month, beating [John Cheruiyot Korir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Cheruiyot_Korir "John Cheruiyot Korir") to the continental title. As African champion, he was selected to represent the continental at the [2002 IAAF World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_IAAF_World_Cup "2002 IAAF World Cup"). He took the [5000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres")[silver medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_medal "Silver medal") behind the reigning European champion [Alberto García](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alberto_Garc%C3%ADa_(athlete) "Alberto García (athlete)") (who was banned in 2003 for taking [EPO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erythropoietin "Erythropoietin")).[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei#cite_note-12) Among Kosgei's other honours that year was a silver medal from the [World Military Track and Field Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Military_Track_and_Field_Championships "World Military Track and Field Championships").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei#cite_note-IAAFBio-2)

### Road running world record

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Road running world record")]

After a relatively quiet 2003, Kosgei again came to the fore by setting a [world record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_world_records_in_athletics "List of world records in athletics") for the 25 km road distance, winning the [BIG 25 Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BIG_25_Berlin "BIG 25 Berlin") race in 1:12:45 on 9 May 2004 (a record which stood until 2010 when it was beaten by [Samuel Kosgei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Kosgei "Samuel Kosgei") at the same race).[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei#cite_note-13)

Kosgei won the [Berlin Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Half_Marathon "Berlin Half Marathon") in 2006, setting a half marathon personal best of 59:07 minutes as well as bettering his marks over 15 km and 20 km along the way.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei#cite_note-IAAFBio-2) He competed at the 2007 [Hamburg Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamburg_Marathon "Hamburg Marathon") and [Amsterdam Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam_Marathon "Amsterdam Marathon"), finishing 14th and 10th, respectively. Kosgei was one of four men under an hour at the [Rotterdam Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotterdam_Half_Marathon "Rotterdam Half Marathon") in 2008 and his time of 59:37 brought him fourth place.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei#cite_note-14) He took three consecutive wins at the [Amatrice-Configno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amatrice-Configno?action=edit&redlink=1 "Amatrice-Configno (page does not exist)") road race from 2008 to 2010, building upon his first win in 2003.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei#cite_note-15) He posted a personal record of 2:09:12 hours at the 2008 [Paris Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Marathon "Paris Marathon"), where he finished eighth.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei#cite_note-16)

He scored his first victory over the marathon distance at the [Maratona d'Italia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maratona_d'Italia "Maratona d'Italia") in October 2010, where he set a new course record of 2:09:00.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei#cite_note-Carpi-17)

Kosgei is married and has two children. He is currently coached by Italian [Gabriele Nicola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabriele_Nicola?action=edit&redlink=1 "Gabriele Nicola (page does not exist)").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei#cite_note-Carpi-17)

**Paul Malakwen Kosgei** (born 22 April 1978, in [Marakwet](link_13)) is a Kenyan [long-distance](link_14) and [marathon](link_15) runner. He first came to prominence in athletics by taking the World Junior Record of 3000m steeple in 1997, and later with consecutive medals at the [IAAF World Cross Country Championships](link_2) from 1998 to 2000.

In 1999 he started his technical collaboration with the Italian Coach Renato Canova, that changed his event, looking at longer distances.

He made his debut at the [IAAF World Half Marathon Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "IAAF World Half Marathon Championships") in 2002 and became the surprise world champion for the event. Later that year he became the African champion on the track in the [10,000 metres](link_16) and also won [silver medals](link_17) at the [2002 Commonwealth Games](link_11) and [2002 IAAF World Cup](link_18).

He focused entirely on [road running](link_19) after 2002 and he broke the [world record](link_20) for the 25 km distance, running 1:12:45 in May 2004. His personal best over the [half marathon](link_21) (59:07 minutes), with which he won the 2006 [Berlin Half Marathon](link_22), ranks him within the top ten fastest ever over the distance.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei#cite_note-1) He began to focus on marathon running and won his first race at the [Maratona d'Italia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maratona_d [link_23]'Italia "Maratona d'Italia") in 2010 with a course record and personal best time of 2:09.00.

From 2009 there was a passage of coach, from Renato Canova to Gabriele Nicola, who is a student of the former coach.

### Junior world record and first medals

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Junior world record and first medals")]

Kosgei started his international career as a [cross country runner](link_24) and a [steeplechaser](link_25). He came to prominence as a junior athlete in 1997 when he took the junior [bronze medal](link_26) at the [1997 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](link_27), and he also reached the [1997 IAAF Grand Prix Final](link_28) for the [3000 metres steeplechase](link_29). He established his pedigree by setting a [world junior record](link_30) for the event.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei#cite_note-IAAFBio-2)

He emerged as a senior the following year, taking the bronze in the short race at the [1998 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](link_4) and helping Kenya to the team [gold medal](link_31).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei#cite_note-IAAFBio-2) He also led Kenya to a team victory at the [IAAF World Road Relay Championships](link_32) in [Manaus](link_33) in April.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei#cite_note-3) He was the fourth fastest athlete in the world that year in the steeplechase. He also began taking part in [road running](link_19) competitions and won the 10 km [BOclassic](link_34) race at the end of the year.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei#cite_note-4) He improved to the [silver medal](link_17) position at the [1999 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](link_3), finishing behind [Paul Tergat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat "Paul Tergat") to help Kenya to a consecutive team win. He represented his country on the track at the [1999 World Championships in Athletics](link_35) in [Seville](link_36), where he was seventh in the men's steeplechase. He closed his track season with a fifth-place finish at the [1999 IAAF Grand Prix Final](link_37).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei#cite_note-IAAFBio-2)

### African and World Champion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: African and World Champion")]

From 2000 onwards he later began concentrating on [long-distance running](link_14) and dropped his steeplechase speciality. He set a 10 km best of 27:40 to win the [Parelloop](link_38) race in [Brunssum](link_39) that year.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei#cite_note-5) He also took a third consecutive cross country medal at the [2000 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](link_5), continuing the streak of Kenya team victories with his bronze medal performance.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei#cite_note-IAAFBio-2) He took road circuit wins in Europe at the [Giro Podistico Internazionale di Pettinengo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giro_Podistico_Internazionale_di_Pettinengo?action=edit&redlink=1 "Giro Podistico Internazionale di Pettinengo (page does not exist)"), winning the 9.5 km race in 27:03,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei#cite_note-6) and also at the [Giro al Sas](link_40) 10K in [Trento](link_41).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei#cite_note-7) He ran for Kenya in the long race at the [2001 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](link_42) but could not match his short course form and finished in fifth place. The greater distances also did not bring him medals at the [2001 World Championships in Athletics](link_43) as he finished seventh in the [10,000 metres](link_16) final.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei#cite_note-IAAFBio-2) He was the winner of the 2001 [Giro Media Blenio](link_44) 10K race in [Dongio](link_45), recording a time of 28:13.4.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei#cite_note-8)

The 2002 marked a significant breakthrough for Kosgei in both track and road running. In May, he led the Kenyan team to victory at the [2002 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships](link_6) with a time of 1:00:39. He edged out [Jaouad Gharib](link_46) to win the race on his first attempt at the [half marathon](link_21) distance. His first time success did not make him an immediate convert, however: "I have changed my focus from the steeplechase to the 10,000 metres ... Maybe in two or three years I will start to think about running the marathon".[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei#cite_note-9) Kosgei became the Kenyan champion over 10,000 m that summer,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei#cite_note-10) and his next test came at the [2002 Commonwealth Games](link_12) in Manchester, England. He was entered into the 10,000 m race and was second behind his Kenyan compatriot [Wilberforce Talel](link_47) – Kosgei's finishing time of 27:45.46 was seven hundredths of a second behind Talel, who broke the [Games record](link_48) for the event.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei#cite_note-11)

He went unbeaten over the distance at the [2002 African Championships in Athletics](link_8) the following month, beating [John Cheruiyot Korir](link_49) to the continental title. As African champion, he was selected to represent the continental at the [2002 IAAF World Cup](link_18). He took the [5000 metres](link_50)[silver medal](link_17) behind the reigning European champion [Alberto García](link_51) (who was banned in 2003 for taking [EPO](link_52)).[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei#cite_note-12) Among Kosgei's other honours that year was a silver medal from the [World Military Track and Field Championships](link_53).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei#cite_note-IAAFBio-2)

### Road running world record

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Road running world record")]

After a relatively quiet 2003, Kosgei again came to the fore by setting a [world record](link_20) for the 25 km road distance, winning the [BIG 25 Berlin](link_54) race in 1:12:45 on 9 May 2004 (a record which stood until 2010 when it was beaten by [Samuel Kosgei](link_55) at the same race).[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei#cite_note-13)

Kosgei won the [Berlin Half Marathon](link_22) in 2006, setting a half marathon personal best of 59:07 minutes as well as bettering his marks over 15 km and 20 km along the way.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Malakwen_Kosgei#cite_note-IAAFBio-2) He competed at the 2007 [Hamburg Marathon](link_56) and [Amsterdam Marathon](link_57), finishing 14th and 10th, respectively. **Kenenisa Bekele Beyecha**[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-4) ([Oromo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oromo_language "Oromo language"): _Qananiisaa baqqalaa_; [Amharic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amharic_language "Amharic language"): ቀነኒሳ በቀለ; born 13 June 1982) is an Ethiopian [long-distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_running "Long-distance running"). He was the world record holder in both the [5,000-metre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres") and [10,000-metre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10000_metres "10000 metres") from 2004 until 2020. He won the gold medal in both the [5,000 m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2008_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_5000_metres "Athletics at the 2008 Summer Olympics – Men's 5000 metres") and [10,000 m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2008_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_10,000_metres "Athletics at the 2008 Summer Olympics – Men's 10,000 metres") events at the [2008 Beijing Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Summer_Olympics "2008 Summer Olympics"). At the [2004 Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Summer_Olympics "2004 Summer Olympics"), he won the gold medal in the [10,000 m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2004_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_10,000_metres "Athletics at the 2004 Summer Olympics – Men's 10,000 metres") and the silver medal in the [5,000 m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2004_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_5000_metres "Athletics at the 2004 Summer Olympics – Men's 5000 metres").

He is the most successful runner in the history of the [IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "IAAF World Cross Country Championships"), with six long (12 km) course and five short (4 km) course titles. He won the 10,000 m title at the [World Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Championships_in_Athletics "World Championships in Athletics") in 2003, 2005, 2007 and 2009 (matching [Haile Gebrselassie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie "Haile Gebrselassie")'s four in a row win streak). Kenenisa was unbeaten over 10,000 m from his debut in 2003 until 2011, when he failed to finish at the World Championships final.

At the [2009 World Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2009 World Championships in Athletics") he became the first man to win both 5000 m and 10,000 m title at the same championships. Over 5000 m he has also won an Olympic silver (2004), World Championship bronze (2003), two [African Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Championships_in_Athletics "African Championships in Athletics") titles and one [All-Africa Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All-Africa_Games "All-Africa Games") gold medal. He also won the [3000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3000_metres "3000 metres") title at the [2006 World Indoor Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_IAAF_World_Indoor_Championships "2006 IAAF World Indoor Championships").

On 6 April 2014, he produced the sixth fastest marathon debut ever on a record-eligible course with his victory at the [Paris Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Marathon "Paris Marathon"), in a course record time of 2:05:04. On 25 September 2016, Kenenisa won the [Berlin Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Marathon "Berlin Marathon") in a time of 2:03:03, a new personal best, then the third-fastest marathon of all time. On 29 September 2019, he again won the Berlin Marathon in a time of 2:01:41, two seconds slower than [the then world record of 2:01:39](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon_world_record_progression "Marathon world record progression") set by [Eliud Kipchoge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge "Eliud Kipchoge") in the 2018 Berlin Marathon.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-5) Considering his accomplishments in cross country, track, and road racing, many consider him to be the greatest distance runner of all time.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-8)

Kenenisa Bekele was born in 1982 in [Bekoji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bekoji "Bekoji") in the [Arsi Zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arsi_Zone "Arsi Zone") of [Oromia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oromia "Oromia") Region, the same town as several other prominent long-distance runners, including the Dibaba's Daughters ([Ejegayehu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ejegayehu_Dibaba "Ejegayehu Dibaba"), [Tirunesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tirunesh_Dibaba "Tirunesh Dibaba") and [Genzebe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genzebe_Dibaba "Genzebe Dibaba")) and their cousin [Derartu Tulu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derartu_Tulu "Derartu Tulu").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-9) Kenenisa was born the second child to parents who made a living as [barley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barley "Barley") farmers, along with three brothers and two sisters.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-:0-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-11) The family practiced [Ethiopian Orthodox Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopian_Orthodox_Tewahedo_Church "Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-:0-10)

Kenenisa initially aspired to a career in medicine, education, or the civil service.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-:1-12) He began to train seriously in running with the encouragement of a physical education teacher, while drawing inspiration from the success of Derartu Tulu and [Haile Gebrselassie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie "Haile Gebrselassie").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-:1-12) Kenenisa achieved his first medals at an international competition with second-place finishes in both the 3000 metres of the [1999 World Youth Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_World_Youth_Championships_in_Athletics "1999 World Youth Championships in Athletics") and the 5000 metres of the [2000 World Junior Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_World_Junior_Championships_in_Athletics_%E2%80%93_Men's_200_metres "2000 World Junior Championships in Athletics – Men's 200 metres").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-:2-13) He won his first gold medal in the junior race of the [2001 World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships_%E2%80%93_Junior_men's_race "2001 IAAF World Cross Country Championships – Junior men's race").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-:2-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-14) His success in running enabled him to purchase a house and to help fund his siblings' educations.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-15)

### 2001 – 2003: Early career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kenenisa_Bekele&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 2001 – 2003: Early career")]

In August 2001, Kenenisa set a [3000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3000_metres "3000 metres")[world junior record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_junior_world_records_in_athletics "List of junior world records in athletics") by running 7:30.67 minutes in [Brussels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brussels "Brussels"). The record lasted for three and a half years, being broken by [Augustine Choge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_Choge "Augustine Choge") with a run of 7:28.78 minutes.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-16) In December 2000 and 2001 Kenenisa won the 15k roadrace Montferland Run in the Netherlands.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-WA-17) For five years in a row, from 2002 (at the age of 19) through 2006, he took both short (4 km) and long (12 km) races at the [IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "IAAF World Cross Country Championships"), a feat no other runner has accomplished even once.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-18) After the IAAF eliminated the short course race in 2007, Kenenisa won a final long course race in 2008, bringing his World Cross Country medal totals to 11 senior individual gold medals (6 long course, 5 short course), 1 senior silver medal (2001), 1 junior gold medal (2001), 2 team gold medals (2004, 2005), 3 team silver medals (2002, 2003, & 2008), and 1 team bronze medal (2006) for a grand total of 19 medals.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-WA-17)

Kenenisa became known for his ability to accelerate very quickly at the end of a long-distance race; in [Oslo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo "Oslo") in June 2003, he chased after [Kenyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya")[Abraham Chebii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Chebii "Abraham Chebii") and won the race in 12:52.26.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-WA-17) He has faced fellow Ethiopian, [Haile Gebrselassie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie "Haile Gebrselassie"), twice in road competition, once in cross country, and six times on the track. Haile defeated Kenenisa on the track in the 2000 Nurnberg 5000 metres, the 2001 [Great Ethiopian Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Ethiopian_Run "Great Ethiopian Run") 10 km, and the [Cross de l'Acier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_de_l'Acier "Cross de l'Acier") in December 2001, but lost to Kenenisa in [Hengelo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hengelo "Hengelo") 2003 over 10,000 m (26:53 to 26:54), Rome 2003 over 5000 m (12:57 to 13:00), Paris [2003 World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2003 World Championships in Athletics") over 10,000 m (26:49 to 26:50), [Athens 2004 Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athens_2004_Olympic_Games "Athens 2004 Olympic Games") (27:05 to 27:27), in the 10,000 m in the [Beijing 2008 Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing_2008_Olympic_Games "Beijing 2008 Olympic Games") (27:01 to 27:06), and in the [Great North Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_North_Run "Great North Run")[half marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon "Half marathon") in September 2013 (60:09 to 60:41).

In 2004, Kenenisa broke the world records for the indoor 5000 m, outdoor 5000 m and outdoor 10,000 m (both in a timeframe of 9 days).[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-19) He won the short and long course world cross country titles, leading Ethiopia to the senior men's team title. He also won a gold medal in the men's 10,000 metres and a silver medal in the men's 5000 metres in the 2004 Olympic Games in [Athens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athens "Athens").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-20)

On 4 January 2005, Kenenisa's fiancée, 18-year-old Alem Techale, died of an apparent heart attack while on a training run with him. Although it was initially stated that no [autopsy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autopsy "Autopsy") was performed, Alem's and Kenenisa's manager [Jos Hermens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos_Hermens "Jos Hermens") later said that an autopsy had revealed nothing conclusive about Techale's death. She was the [2003 World Youth Champion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_World_Youth_Championships_in_Athletics "2003 World Youth Championships in Athletics") in the [1500 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1500_metres "1500 metres") and in excellent physical condition.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-21)

[![Image 36](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d1/Kenenisa_Bekele_-_Smiling.jpg/250px-Kenenisa_Bekele_-_Smiling.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kenenisa_Bekele_-_Smiling.jpg)

Kenenisa competing in the 2006 Golden League.

He resumed racing on 29 January, and lost indoors over 3000 m to Ireland's [Alistair Cragg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alistair_Cragg "Alistair Cragg") after sprinting towards the line with one and a half laps to go, while thinking that there was only half a lap left.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-22) A few weeks later he lost to fellow Ethiopian [Markos Geneti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markos_Geneti "Markos Geneti") over [two miles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two_miles "Two miles").

In March, Kenenisa lined up to defend his long and short course titles at the [2005 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "2005 IAAF World Cross Country Championships"). He won on the short course despite a fast pace set by [Qatari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qatar "Qatar")[Saif Saaeed Shaheen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saif_Saaeed_Shaheen "Saif Saaeed Shaheen"), and followed that win with a long course victory the next day over [Eritrean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eritrea "Eritrea")[Zersenay Tadese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zersenay_Tadese "Zersenay Tadese") and Kenyan rival [Eliud Kipchoge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge "Eliud Kipchoge").

On 8 August 2005, Kenenisa Bekele won the [gold medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_medal "Gold medal") in the 10,000 m at the [2005 World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2005 World Championships in Athletics") in Helsinki with a last [200 m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/200_m "200 m") spurt.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-23) On 26 August 2005, Kenenisa set the [10,000 m world record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_record_progression_10000_metres_men "World record progression 10000 metres men") 26:17.53 at the 29th [Memorial Van Damme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memorial_Van_Damme "Memorial Van Damme") meeting in [Brussels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brussels "Brussels"), slicing nearly three seconds off his previous world record 26:20.31, and running with 5000 m splits of 13:09 and 13:08 minutes.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-24) The race saw 6 runners finishing in less than 27 minutes, with Sammy Wanjiru dipping in 26:41.75, a new world junior record. At the end of 2005 Kenenisa was voted the _[Track & Field News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Track\_&\_Field\_News "Track & Field News")_ magazine athlete of the year for the second year in a row.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-25)

[![Image 37](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7d/Kenenisa_Bekele_running.jpg/250px-Kenenisa_Bekele_running.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kenenisa_Bekele_running.jpg)

Kenenisa leading the way at the 2007 Cross de Itálica.

When Kenenisa won the 3000 m at the [2006 IAAF World Indoor Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_IAAF_World_Indoor_Championships "2006 IAAF World Indoor Championships") in [Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow "Moscow"), he became the first athlete in history to be Olympic champion, world outdoor track champion, world indoor track champion, and world cross country champion.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-26) In 2006 he won five out of six [IAAF Golden League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_Golden_League "IAAF Golden League") events (5000 m) in the same season, which earned him a total of US$83,333.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-27)

On 17 February 2007, he broke the indoor world record over 2000 m in [Birmingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham "Birmingham"), with a time of 4:49.99. His spectacular final 300 m aided this time which would be considered excellent even outdoors.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-28) On 24 March 2007, however, his streak of 27 consecutive victories in cross country races (dating back to his last previous loss in December 2001) came to an end when after leading the race in the penultimate lap of the [2007 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "2007 IAAF World Cross Country Championships") in [Mombasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mombasa "Mombasa") he succumbed to the very hot, humid conditions (which caused more than 1/6 of all competitors to drop out) and was passed by eventual winner [Zersenay Tadese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zersenay_Tadese "Zersenay Tadese") on the last lap before Kenenisa dropped out. This was greeted with cheers by the Kenyan crowds, an occurrence which has been frowned upon by the wider athletics community.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-29)

He recovered from that rare failure to take the 10,000-metre title at the [2007 IAAF World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_IAAF_World_Championships "2007 IAAF World Championships") in [Osaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osaka "Osaka"), once again besting his compatriot [Sileshi Sihine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sileshi_Sihine "Sileshi Sihine"). During that race, he looked like he was going to be dropped several times over the last 800 metres, but recovered to overtake Sileshi with 150 metres to go and take his third straight world title.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-30)

### 2008: Beijing Olympics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kenenisa_Bekele&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 2008: Beijing Olympics")]

[![Image 38](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4a/Kenenisa_Bekele_Berlin_2009.jpg/250px-Kenenisa_Bekele_Berlin_2009.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kenenisa_Bekele_Berlin_2009.jpg)

Celebrating his gold medal victory at the 2009 World Championships.

In [Edinburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edinburgh "Edinburgh") on 30 March 2008, he won his sixth World Cross Country title (long course – 12k), breaking the three-way tie of 5 wins he had previously shared with [Paul Tergat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat "Paul Tergat") and [John Ngugi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Ngugi "John Ngugi"). With this win, Kenenisa laid sole claim to most decorated athlete in [IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "IAAF World Cross Country Championships") history. He has won 6 long course (12k) individual gold medals, 5 short course (4k) gold medals, 1 junior championship (8k), and 4 team gold medals for a sum total of 16 gold medals. His overall medal count (both individual and team results) stands at 27 medals: 16 gold, 9 silver and 2 bronze.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-31)

On 17 August 2008 Kenenisa won gold in the 10,000m finals with a time of 27:01.17, setting a new [Olympic Record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_records_in_athletics "List of Olympic records in athletics") in the process. In a race in which 20 men broke the 28-minute barrier and four finished under his 2004 Olympic record of 27:05.10, he needed his renowned finishing kick to pull out the victory, running a 53.42-second final 400 metres (similar to the 53.02-second final 400-metre sprint he used to win the gold medal in Athens in 2004 over the same distance).[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-BBC-32)

On 23 August 2008 Kenenisa bested his competitors and won the 5000-metre finals, shattering [Saïd Aouita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sa%C3%AFd_Aouita "Saïd Aouita")'s Olympic Record by almost eight seconds with a time of 12:57.82. The race was remarkable for his manner of doing most of the pacing himself before accelerating to a scintillating finish: his last 3000 metres only took 7:35.53, his final 2000 metres 4:56.97, last 1600 metres 3:57.01 (=3:58.4 final mile) and his final lap a punishing 53.87 seconds.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-33) By winning the 10,000/5000m double in the Beijing Olympics, Kenenisa joined another elite group of athletes: [Hannes Kolehmainen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannes_Kolehmainen "Hannes Kolehmainen") (1912), [Emil Zátopek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emil_Z%C3%A1topek "Emil Zátopek") (1952), [Vladimir Kuts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Kuts "Vladimir Kuts") (1956), [Lasse Virén](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lasse_Vir%C3%A9n "Lasse Virén") (twice, in 1972 and 1976) and [Miruts Yifter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miruts_Yifter "Miruts Yifter") (1980).[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-34)

### 2009: Berlin World Championships

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kenenisa_Bekele&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: 2009: Berlin World Championships")]

Kenenisa Bekele won two gold medals at the [2009 World Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2009 World Championships in Athletics"), held in Berlin. His double victories in 5000m (13:17.09) and 10,000m (26:46.31 – a World Championships Record) were unprecedented and by doing this became the first man to take both the long-distance track gold medals at the same World Championships.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-35) His talent combination of endurance and speed has made it nearly impossible to defeat Kenenisa when he is at full strength. During the 10,000m race in which he was running behind Eritrea's Zersenay Tadesse, the broadcaster declared "it is over, in fact it was over from the start" as the final lap began and Kenenisa turned an ostensibly close race into a blowout. The IAAF announcer concluded, "this man is probably the greatest distance runner we will ever see."[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-36)

In spite of his unrivalled success in athletics, Kenenisa did not experience the mainstream appeal that others such as Haile Gebrselassie did. His quiet demeanour and aversion to interviews did not make him a highly marketable athlete in the [Western world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_world "Western world"). Fellow [world record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_world_records_in_athletics "List of world records in athletics") holder [Usain Bolt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Usain_Bolt "Usain Bolt") stated that Kenenisa Bekele's achievements had not received the recognition that they deserved.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-37)

[![Image 39](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8d/Men%27s_10000m_Final_-_2012_Olympics_-_4.jpg/250px-Men%27s_10000m_Final_-_2012_Olympics_-_4.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Men's_10000m_Final_-_2012_Olympics_-_4.jpg)

 Kenenisa pursuing the lead pack in the Men's 10,000 metres final event at the 2012 Summer Olympics.

Kenenisa made a disappointing start to 2010, finishing fourth in the [Edinburgh Cross Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edinburgh_Cross_Country "Edinburgh Cross Country") in a race he was favored to win – a trio of Kenyan athletes ran him out of the contest over the final lap. He spent the entirety of the indoor and outdoor seasons out with a ruptured calf muscle.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-38)

### 2011 World Championships and 2012 Olympics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kenenisa_Bekele&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: 2011 World Championships and 2012 Olympics")]

Kenenisa Bekele finally returned to training after a knee injury in March 2011.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-39) Having not raced on the track since 2009, Kenenisa returned for the World Championships.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-40) He dropped out of the 10,000m with 10 laps remaining.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-41) Kenenisa decided not to run the 5000 m and[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-42) returned to the Diamond League at the [Ivo Van Damme Memorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivo_Van_Damme_Memorial "Ivo Van Damme Memorial") in Brussels where he set the fastest time in the world for the 10,000 metres in 2011.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-43)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-44)

Kenenisa's 2012 season did not start well, as he was a lowly eleventh place at the Edinburgh Cross Country.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-45) In April, he appeared to have returned to form by winning the [Great Ireland Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Ireland_Run "Great Ireland Run") in a new personal best time for a 10 km road race of 27:49, improving the course record by 46 seconds.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-46)

In the [2012 London Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Summer_Olympics "2012 Summer Olympics")[10,000m race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2012_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_10,000_metres "Athletics at the 2012 Summer Olympics – Men's 10,000 metres") he ran within the leading group for the whole race, but could not keep up with the [Mo Farah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mo_Farah "Mo Farah")'s sprint in the last 150 metres and eventually finished fourth, with a time of 27:32.44, just 1.01 second outside the bronze medalist, his brother [Tariku](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tariku_Bekele "Tariku Bekele").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-47)

In his first race of 2013 he won the Great Ireland Run for a second time.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-48) Kenenisa then won the Great North Run half marathon in a time of 60:09, beating Mo Farah by just one second after making a move that Farah couldn't match with just less than 12 miles gone.

[![Image 40](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/53/Kenenisa_Bekele_2014_Paris_Marathon_t084500.jpg/250px-Kenenisa_Bekele_2014_Paris_Marathon_t084500.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kenenisa_Bekele_2014_Paris_Marathon_t084500.jpg)

Kenenisa Bekele at the 2014 Paris Marathon

2014 - 2015
Kenenisa Bekele started his marathon career in the [2014 Paris Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Marathon#2014 "Paris Marathon") on 6 April 2014. His marathon debut was very successful as he bettered both the Paris course record and the debut marathon times of past legends Haile Gebrselassie, Paul Tergat and Samuel Wanjiru by running 2:05:04 to win.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-Letsrun.com-49) Kenenisa then went on to compete in the [2014 Chicago Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Chicago_Marathon "2014 Chicago Marathon") on 12 October 2014. He finished fourth in 2:05:51, 1min 40s behind Kenya's [Eliud Kipchoge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge "Eliud Kipchoge").[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-nbcsports.com-50) On 23 January 2015, Kenenisa took on the [Dubai Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dubai_Marathon "Dubai Marathon"), where he had to retire from the race after 30 km.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-dubaimarathon.org-51) He was planned to compete in the [2015 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_London_Marathon "2015 London Marathon") but had to withdraw due to a persistent injury to his right [Achilles tendon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Achilles_tendon "Achilles tendon").[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-runnersworld.com-52)

Following 11 months of injury, Kenenisa returned to racing at the [2016 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_London_Marathon "2016 London Marathon"). Prior to the race he indicated he was only currently at 90% fitness. Kenenisa finished in 3rd place behind winner Eliud Kipchoge and runner-up [Stanley Biwott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Biwott "Stanley Biwott") in a time of 2:06:36. This performance was despite the fact he only returned to jogging in early 2016 following injury and had only completed 6 weeks of specific marathon training. He was also hampered in the race by missing his drinks at 5 separate stations, due to them being used by the designated pacemakers.

2016 - 2017
On 24 April, he placed third at the [2016 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_London_Marathon "2016 London Marathon") with a time of two hours six minutes and 38 seconds. In September he won the [2016 Berlin Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Berlin_Marathon "2016 Berlin Marathon") in a time of 2:03:03 which set a new personal best time for him at the [Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon") distance and the second fastest marathon of all time.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-53) On 19 January 2017, attempting to break the world record, Kenenisa dropped out of the Dubai Marathon after the half way mark due to a fall at the beginning of the race.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-54) On 23 April 2017, Kenenisa finished second in the [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_London_Marathon "2017 London Marathon"), finishing in 2:05:57, 9 seconds behind winner [Daniel Wanjiru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Wanjiru "Daniel Wanjiru").[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-55)

Kenenisa's outstanding track career led to his involvement in a project to break the two-hour barrier for the marathon, though a number of factors undermined this effort.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-NYT_2hour-56)

2018 - 2019
Kenenisa ran the 2018 [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Marathon "London Marathon") in April and came in sixth place with a time of 2:08:53.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-57) He also ran the Amsterdam marathon in October 2018 but dropped out due to injury with about 2 km to go.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-58) Kenenisa won the [2019 Berlin Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Berlin_Marathon "2019 Berlin Marathon") in September in 2:01:41, the second fastest time ever at the time and just two seconds off of the world record set by [Eliud Kipchoge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge "Eliud Kipchoge") on the same course the previous year. After the run he stated that he still believes that he can break the world record.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-59)

2020 - 2021
Kenenisa won the London half marathon on 1 March 2020 in 60:22. He improved on the course record set by [Mo Farah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mo_Farah "Mo Farah") in 2019 by 1:18. [Chris Thompson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Thompson_(runner) "Chris Thompson (runner)") came in second with 61:07, also within the former course record.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-60)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-61) Kenenisa returned to the [Berlin Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Berlin_Marathon "2021 Berlin Marathon") in September, where he placed third in 2:06:47. The race was won by his compatriot [Guye Adola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guye_Adola "Guye Adola") in 2:05:45, while Kenya's [Bethwel Yegon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bethwel_Yegon "Bethwel Yegon") finished second.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-62) In November, he finished six at the [2021 New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_New_York_City_Marathon "2021 New York City Marathon") with a time of 2:12:52.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-WAprofile-2)

2022 - 2023
In September, he placed third at the Great North Run half marathon in a time of 1:01:01.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-WAprofile-2) The next month, Kenenisa competed in the [2022 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_London_Marathon "2022 London Marathon"), finishing fifth in 2:05:53 to set a masters world record in age 40 group.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-63) In April, he took part in the London Marathon but withdrew from the race after 25k mark. Then, in October, he announced on Instagram that he had departed from the NN running team and transitioned his sponsorship from Nike to Anta, a Chinese sports brand. In December, Kenenisa took part in the Valencia Marathon. Although he fell behind the leading group before reaching the 15 km mark, he managed to finish fourth in a M40 Master World Record with a time of 2:04:19. This achievement solidifies him as the first athlete aged over 40 to complete a marathon in sub 2:05 clocking.

The 41-year-old Kenenisa competed in the [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_London_Marathon "2024 London Marathon") on 21 April 2024, where he finished second behind [Alexander Munyao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Mutiso_Munyao "Alexander Mutiso Munyao") breaking his own Masters record by 4 seconds running 2:04:15.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-64) Kenenisa was selected to represent Ethiopia in the [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2024_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_marathon "Athletics at the 2024 Summer Olympics – Men's marathon") at the [2024 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Summer_Olympics "2024 Summer Olympics"). At 41 years of age, it was his fourth Olympic appearance and first time competing at the event since the 2012 London Olympics.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-65) Kenenisa ended up finishing in 39th place with a time of 2:12:24[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-66)

On 18 November 2007, Kenenisa married [Ethiopian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopians "Ethiopians") film actress Danawit Gebregziabher in Addis Ababa.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-67) Kenenisa has one younger brother, [Tariku Bekele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tariku_Bekele "Tariku Bekele"), who is also an accomplished world-class distance runner.

**Ferenc Szekeres** (born 21 March 1947) is a retired [long-distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_runner "Long-distance runner") from [Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary "Hungary"), who twice won the [Amsterdam Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam_Marathon "Amsterdam Marathon"), in 1979 and 1981. He represented his native country in at two [Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer_Olympics "Summer Olympics"): 1972 and 1980.

**Ferenc Szekeres** (born 21 March 1947) is a retired [long-distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_runner "Long-distance runner") from [Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary "Hungary"), who twice won the [Amsterdam Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam_Marathon "Amsterdam Marathon"), in 1979 and 1981. He represented his native country in at two [Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer_Olympics "Summer Olympics"): 1972 and 1980.

**Paul Kipsiele Koech** (born 10 November 1981) is a Kenyan runner who specializes in the [3000 metres steeplechase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3000_metres_steeplechase "3000 metres steeplechase"). He won the [2004 Olympic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Summer_Olympics "2004 Summer Olympics")[bronze medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronze_medal "Bronze medal") in this event. His personal best of 7:54.31 minutes is the third fastest of all time.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kipsiele_Koech#cite_note-1)

He was born in 1981 in [Kapchepkoro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kapchepkoro?action=edit&redlink=1 "Kapchepkoro (page does not exist)"), near the town of [Sotik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sotik "Sotik"). He graduated from Cheplanget Secondary School in 1999. He did well at the National Cross Country Championships and was subsequently invited to compete in Europe and joined a team managed by [James Templeton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Templeton "James Templeton").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kipsiele_Koech#cite_note-focus-2)

Despite being among the fastest steeplechasers, he has failed several times at the Kenyan trials for World championships or Olympics.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kipsiele_Koech#cite_note-confident-3) He competed at the all seven [IAAF World Athletics Final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Athletics_Final "IAAF World Athletics Final") meetings, finishing every time in the top three, being the only athlete to achieve it.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kipsiele_Koech#cite_note-4)

He has had success in [cross country running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_country_running "Cross country running"), with wins at the [Cinque Mulini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinque_Mulini "Cinque Mulini") (2006) and the [Iris Lotto Cross Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iris_Lotto_Cross_Cup "Iris Lotto Cross Cup") (2007) to his name. He holds the steeplechase meet record for the [Prefontaine Classic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prefontaine_Classic "Prefontaine Classic"), [Adidas Grand Prix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adidas_Grand_Prix "Adidas Grand Prix"), and [DN Galan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DN_Galan "DN Galan").

He has built a primary school near his home. He also trains some younger runners, including World junior champion [Mercy Cherono](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercy_Cherono "Mercy Cherono").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kipsiele_Koech#cite_note-confident-3) Koech is married and has a daughter born in 2004 and a younger son.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kipsiele_Koech#cite_note-focus-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kipsiele_Koech#cite_note-confident-3)

In February 2010 he set a world best of 5:17.04 in the rarely competed 2000 m indoor steeplechase.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kipsiele_Koech#cite_note-5) He won twice in the [2010 Diamond League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Diamond_League "2010 Diamond League") and finished with enough points to become the inaugural steeplechase Diamond Trophy winner. He improved his indoor 2000 m steeplechase record to 5:13.77 at the [Indoor Flanders Meeting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indoor_Flanders_Meeting "Indoor Flanders Meeting") in February 2011.

At the Rome [Diamond League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_IAAF_Diamond_League "2012 IAAF Diamond League") event in May Koech set a new personal best of 7:54.31, the third fastest time ever for the 3000 metre steeplechase.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kipsiele_Koech#cite_note-6) Despite this performance, he did not perform well in the altitude of the Kenyan Olympic trials and finished outside of the top five.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kipsiele_Koech#cite_note-7)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Kenyan steeplechase runner (born 1981)

Not to be confused with [Paul Koech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Koech "Paul Koech").

Paul Kipsiele Koech[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/01/Paul_Kipsiele_Koech_2010_Memorial_Van_Damme.jpg/250px-Paul_Kipsiele_Koech_2010_Memorial_Van_Damme.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Paul_Kipsiele_Koech_2010_Memorial_Van_Damme.jpg)

**Paul Kipsiele Koech** (born 10 November 1981) is a Kenyan runner who specializes in the [3000 metres steeplechase](link_8). He won the [2004 Olympic](link_9)[bronze medal](link_10) in this event. His personal best of 7:54.31 minutes is the third fastest of all time.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kipsiele_Koech#cite_note-1)

He was born in 1981 in [Kapchepkoro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kapchepkoro?action=edit&redlink=1 "Kapchepkoro (page does not exist)"), near the town of [Sotik](link_11). He graduated from Cheplanget Secondary School in 1999. He did well at the National Cross Country Championships and was subsequently invited to compete in Europe and joined a team managed by [James Templeton](link_12).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kipsiele_Koech#cite_note-focus-2)

Despite being among the fastest steeplechasers, he has failed several times at the Kenyan trials for World championships or Olympics.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kipsiele_Koech#cite_note-confident-3) He competed at the all seven [IAAF World Athletics Final](link_13) meetings, finishing every time in the top three, being the only athlete to achieve it.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kipsiele_Koech#cite_note-4)

He has had success in [cross country running](link_14), with wins at the [Cinque Mulini](link_15) (2006) and the [Iris Lotto Cross Cup](link_16) (2007) to his name. He holds the steeplechase meet record for the [Prefontaine Classic](link_17), [Adidas Grand Prix](link_18), and [DN Galan](link_19).

He has built a primary school near his home. He also trains some younger runners, including World junior champion [Mercy Cherono](link_20).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kipsiele_Koech#cite_note-confident-3) Koech is married and has a daughter born in 2004 and a younger son.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kipsiele_Koech#cite_note-focus-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kipsiele_Koech#cite_note-confident-3)

In February 2010 he set a world best of 5:17.04 in the rarely competed 2000 m indoor steeplechase.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kipsiele_Koech#cite_note-5) He won twice in the [2010 Diamond League](link_2) and finished with enough points to become the inaugural steeplechase Diamond Trophy winner. He improved his indoor 2000 m steeplechase record to 5:13.77 at the [Indoor Flanders Meeting](link_21) in February 2011.

At the Rome [Diamond League](link_22) event in May Koech set a new personal best of 7:54.31, the third fastest time ever for the 3000 metre steeplechase.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kipsiele_Koech#cite_note-6) Despite this performance, he did not perform well in the altitude of the Kenyan Olympic trials and finished outside of the top five.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kipsiele_Koech#cite_note-7)
